edits.text: Also, due to a tone change rule for "不" (bù), the phrase "不会" (bù huì) is actually pronounced "bú huì."
If the speaker wishes to express that they are able to execute an action requiring a consciously studied skill, 会 (huì) can be used instead.
The overlap between them can be broken down into these areas, explained in the sections below:
One pattern this use of 怎么 (zěnme) frequently appears in is with 这么 (zhème) or 那么 (nàme).

You may know that 怎么 (zěnme) can mean "how", but by adding 样 (yàng) to it and making it 怎么样 (zěnmeyàng), you can ask how something is, or what it is like. This is useful in all manner of conversations, and is essential for building conversation skills.

You can use 在 (zài) to express location, but here you will learn how to use 在 (zài) to express location in relation to another object. This way, you can describe if something is "on the table" or "in the room."
Some prepositions can be paired with more abstract concepts to form idiomatic phrases. These kinds of phrases can really make your Chinese sound polished.

Chinese uses measure words, a type of word called classifiers in linguistics which are common in East Asian languages. Measure words have a number of important uses, but one of the first ways you'll need to use them is for counting. Chinese learners should master them, starting with the measure word 个 (gè).
Note: The pinyin for 一起 is written "yīqǐ" but pronounced "yìqǐ" due to a tone change rule.

Certain "psychological verbs" related to feelings or emotional states can be modified with 很 (hěn) to increase their intensity. This is similar to using "really" or "very much" in English. Remember that this only applies to psychological verbs, such as:

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Numbers: 一, 二/两, 三 … 十, 百 and 半
paragraphs: Chinese numbers are simple: 零 0, 一 1, 二 2, 三 3 … 九 9, 十 10, 百 100. Bigger numbers are built from these: 十二 is 12, 二十 is 20, 一百 is 100. 半 means “half”, as in 三点半 (half past three).
When you count things, put a measure word between the number and the noun, such as 三本书. For “two” before a measure word, use 两 (两个孩子). Use 二 when counting or inside bigger numbers (二十).

edits.text: If something happens frequently, two useful words to describe this concept of "often" in Chinese are 常常 (chángcháng) and 往往 (wǎngwǎng). However, they are used in different ways and different places.
Note: The pinyin for 不要 is written "bùyào" but pronounced "búyào" due to a tone change rule.
Rather than just using 在 (zài) to mean "at" a location, you might want to use it to mean "in," "on," or "under" a specific location. To do this, you'll need to add an extra word after the location.

You probably learned early on that 和 (hé) is used as an "and" word to connect nouns and noun phrases,  but not sentences or clauses. This rule is fine for a while but eventually you will begin encountering what appears to be non-nouns linked by 和. Here we look at how you may see 和 used in other ways.

In Chinese, possession is marked with the particle 的 (de), placed after the "owner" noun or noun phrase. This particle works in a similar way to apostrophe-"s" in English, but is used much more broadly in Chinese.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Number + measure word phrases (数量短语)
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun
Subj. + 有 + Number + Measure word + Noun
paragraphs: A 数量短语 (number-measure phrase) tells how many of something there are. In Chinese, a number usually cannot sit directly in front of a noun. You need a measure word in between: 三本书 (three books), 两个孩子 (two children).
Different nouns use different measure words. 个 is the most common and a safe default. 本 is for books, 杯 for cups of drink, 口 for family members, and 块 for yuan.
The phrase goes before the noun, after verbs like 有, 买, 要 or 喝. Use 两, not 二, for 'two' before a measure word.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Sentences with a verb as the predicate
paragraphs: In a Chinese verb-predicate sentence, the verb is the main part of what you say about the subject. Use it to describe actions, wishes and abilities: who does what.
The order is Subject + Verb + Object, like English: 我卖水果 (I sell fruits). Chinese verbs do not change form for person or tense, so 卖 stays 卖.
To make it negative, put 不 before the verb: 他不去医院. For past actions, use 没 instead: 我没看见. Some sentences need no object, like 他能来. Add 吗 at the end to ask a yes/no question: 你想喝水吗？

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Describing things with adjectives
paragraphs: In Chinese, an adjective can be the predicate by itself. You do not add 是 ("to be"). Say 我的家很小, not 我的家是小.

Usually put an adverb like 很 (very) before the adjective. In a plain statement, 很 is often just a light linking word and does not always mean "very". Other degree words, like 非常 or 太, work in the same spot.
To negate, put 不 before the adjective: 我不忙. For contrast, a bare adjective is fine: 这里冷,那里热.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Sentence-final particles: 吧, 了, 吗, 呢
paragraphs: Particles go at the end of a sentence and add tone or meaning. They have no English translation of their own.
吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question: 你会说中文吗？ 吧 makes a suggestion or request sound softer: 多吃些水果吧。 呢 asks "And you?" after you have said something about yourself: 我是中国人,你呢？
了 at the end often shows something has changed or happened: 外边下雨了。 It is also used in 太……了, as in 这个太贵了。 Put 了 before 吗 to ask whether something already happened: 你吃午饭了吗？

edits.text: So for these short sentences, it would be more natural to put 了 after the object. So what are the rules for when to put 了 directly after the verb, and when to put it after the object?

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Statements (陈述句): stating a fact
paragraphs: A statement (陈述句) simply tells the listener something: who does what, who someone is, or what exists. It is the most basic sentence type in Mandarin, and it ends with a full stop, not a question word.

Word order is steady: the subject comes first, then the verb, then the object if there is one. Chinese verbs do not change form, so 我会做菜 stays simple. To make a statement negative, put 不 before the verb, as in 我不喜欢看电视.
Many statements use 是 (to be) or 有 (to have) to link two things, such as 我们是同学 or 他有两个孩子.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Sentences without a subject-predicate pair (非主谓句)
structure: One word or phrase, no subject + predicate
e.g. 喂!  /  车!  /  下雨了。
paragraphs: Most Chinese sentences have a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what it does or is). But some sentences have no such pair. They are called 非主谓句 (fēi zhǔ wèi jù).
Use them for quick reactions, calling out, greeting, or describing weather and events. A single word or short phrase is enough, like 车! (Watch out, a car!) or 下雨了。 (It's raining.)
In your sentence, 喂! is just one word used to get someone's attention, such as when answering the phone or greeting someone. It needs no subject or verb.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Giving commands and requests (imperatives)
paragraphs: An imperative sentence (祈使句) tells someone to do something, or not to. It is used for requests, advice, invitations and orders. Usually there is no subject: the listener, "you", is understood.
Add 请 before the verb to make a polite request, like "please": 请说汉语。 To say "don't", use 别 before the verb, often with 了 at the end: 别说了！
Putting 吧 at the end softens the tone into a gentle suggestion: 多吃些水果吧。

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Asking questions in Chinese
structure: Question word in the answer's place: 谁 / 什么 / 几 / 哪个 / 怎么 / 多少
paragraphs: Chinese questions keep the word order of a statement. You don't move any words around. There are two easy ways to ask.
For a yes/no question, say a full statement and add 吗 at the end: 你有时间吗？ Use it when you expect the answer 'yes' or 'no'.
To ask for specific information, put a question word where the answer would go. 他是谁？ asks about a person, and 这是什么？ asks about a thing. 几 asks about time: 现在几点？ Don't add 吗 to these questions.

edits.text: The verb 有 (yǒu) is negated in a special way. Unlike most verbs, it is negated with 没 (méi) instead of 不 (bù). The negative form of 有 (yǒu) then, is 没有 (méiyǒu).

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Comparing things with 比
structure: 出租车 + 比 + 地铁 + 贵
paragraphs: Use 比 (bǐ) to say that one thing has more of a quality than another. It means "compared to" or "than". For example, A is taller, cheaper or more expensive than B.
Put 比 between the two things you compare, then add an adjective after B. In 出租车比地铁贵, 出租车 is A, 地铁 is B, and 贵 is the quality.
Don't put 很 before the adjective in this pattern. Say 比地铁贵, not 比地铁很贵.
To say A is not more than B, you can use 没有. That is a different pattern, which you will learn later.

edits.text: It is also important to know that you can't use 了 in this type of sentence. 了 only tells you that the action is completed, not any of the other details that this construction is looking for. Since it is already understood that the action took place, the 了 is unhelpful and inappropriate.

Sometimes you can use 的 to really add a kick to your responses, making them stronger. You might even hear Chinese people reply with just 是的 which means "That's right." This usage is similar to the way that English speakers might stress the word "is" in sentences like "It is my food." When used to express affirmation, 会, 能, and 可以 are often used as well. The 是 is optional.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Joining two parallel clauses
paragraphs: 并列复句 means "coordinate compound sentence." You put two short clauses side by side, separated by a comma. Each clause is complete, and the two are equal in importance. No linking word is needed.
Use it to describe two related things together, often to compare or contrast: two people, two places, or two situations. For example, "he does this, I do that."

Build it by writing one full clause, adding a comma (，), then writing a second clause with a similar structure. The second clause often has its own subject. Matching the two parts makes the contrast easy to see.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Exclamatory sentences (感叹句)
paragraphs: An exclamatory sentence (感叹句) shows strong feeling, such as surprise, praise or complaint. In writing it ends with ！.
The most common pattern puts a degree word before an adjective: 太…了 (so/too…), 真… (really…) or 非常… (very…). In 非常好！, 非常 adds strength to 好, so it means "Very good!"
Greetings and farewells like 老师，您好！ and 明天见！ are also said with energy and written with ！. They are set phrases, though, not the adjective pattern above.

edits.text: Note that two o'clock is 两点 (liǎng diǎn), not 二点 (èr diǎn).

了 (le) has many uses.  You probably first learned 了 (le) as a particle that tells you an action is completed, which is also known as "了1." However, this is not about that use of 了 (le); instead, it is about indicating a change of state (了2).  In other words, there is now a new situation, or there is about to be a new situation.  This whole "change of state" idea can take numerous forms, and here are some helpful examples.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Completed actions with verb + 了
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Object
paragraphs: Put 了 right after a verb to show the action was completed. In English, this often matches the past tense: 我买了三本书 means "I bought three books."
A completed action usually comes with a amount, such as 三本 (three) or 十个 (ten). Use 了 when you say how much or how many was done.
To say an action did not happen, use 没 before the verb and drop 了: 我没喝水 (I didn't drink water).

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Yes/no questions with verb + not + verb (正反疑问)
paragraphs: To ask a yes/no question, you can put a verb or adjective together with its negative. This gives the listener two options to choose from: 贵不贵 means "expensive or not expensive?" It sounds neutral and natural, and you don't need 吗 at the end.
For most verbs and adjectives, repeat the word with 不 in the middle: 好看不好看. For 有, the negative is 没有, so you ask 有没有. In the example, 你有没有时间？ means "Do you have time?"
To answer, repeat the verb or adjective: 有 (yes) or 没有 (no).

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Modal verbs: 可能 for 'may / might'
paragraphs: 能愿动词 (modal verbs) are helpers placed before a main verb. They add a meaning such as ability, permission, wish or likelihood. Examples: 能, 会, 可以, 想, 要, 可能.
可能 means 'may' or 'might'. Use it to say something is likely but not certain. Put it right before the verb. To say 'it is impossible', use 不可能 before the verb.
In 天阴了，可能要下雨, 可能 comes before 要下雨 ('is going to rain'). So the speaker is guessing: it may rain.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"1-.title: Asking questions with question words
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么 / 谁 / 哪个?
Subj. + 在 + 哪儿 / 哪里?
几 + Measure word (几点, 星期几)
paragraphs: Mandarin questions with a question word (什么 what, 谁 who, 哪儿 where, 几 how many, 多少 how much, 怎么 how) do not change word order. Put the question word where the answer would go.
他是谁? Answer: 他是老师. 这是什么? Answer: 这是书. The question word simply replaces the missing information.
Use 几 for small numbers, like time, dates and age: 现在几点? Use 多少 for any amount, like prices: 这本书多少钱? Do not add 吗 to these questions.

edits.text: You may know that 怎么 (zěnme) can mean "how", but by adding 样 (yàng) to it and making it 怎么样 (zěnmeyàng), you can ask how something is, or what it is like. This is useful in all manner of conversations, and is essential for building conversation skills.

This doesn't mean that a sentence can never have a question word and 吗 (ma). If a sentence contains verbs of understanding such as 知道 (zhīdào), 了解 (liǎojiě), 明白 (míngbai), 认识 (rènshi), etc., then 吗 (ma) can still be added at the end of the question.
When referring to other people, we can use both the words 人家  (rénjia) and 别人 (biérén). But 人家 has additional grammatical uses which we will explore below.
After briefly reading this, you will know how to use 一下 (yīxià) to express a brief action!
Note: The pinyin for 一下 is written "yīxià" but pronounced "yíxià" due to a tone change rule.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Measure words 层, 封, 件, 条, 位
structure: 买了 + 一条 + 裤子
paragraphs: In Chinese, a number and a noun need a measure word between them. Each measure word goes with certain kinds of nouns. This point covers five of them.

层 is for floors or layers. 封 is for letters. 件 is for clothes on the upper body, and also for matters or things. 条 is for long, thin things, such as pants, rivers, roads and scarves. 位 is a polite word for people, as in 一位老师.
In 我买了一条新裤子, 一条 comes before 新裤子. Pants have two long legs, so they use 条. Add any describing words, like 新, after the measure word.

edits.text: Use this structure to express that "as long as" [something happens], "then" [something else will happen].  In logic, this is referred to as a "sufficient condition," meaning that it may not be the only way to bring about these specific consequences, but it is one reliable way.
Note that 就 (jiù) is often optional.
It's also possible to take the first half of the two-part "if... then..." pattern 如果⋯⋯，就⋯⋯ and make it into a "sandwich pattern" using 如果……的话.

Although the structure above is the best one to learn first, some verbs frequently use 给 but have the 给 coming after the verb, rather than before. It's best to think of these as exceptions to the rule above.

There are a number of structures which can be used to express "not only... but also," including 不但……而且 (bùdàn... érqiě). 不但 can be substituted with 不仅 (bùjǐn) or 不只 (bùzhǐ), both meaning "not only," and can be followed by 而且 (érqiě), 还 (hái), or 也 (yě). Other than 不但……而且 being more common than the others, they are all similar in usage and formality.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Answering the phone with 喂
paragraphs: 喂 (wéi) is an interjection used to get someone's attention. Its most common use is at the start of a phone call, much like "Hello?" in English. It is mainly used on the phone.
Put 喂 first, then pause (a comma in writing) and continue with your sentence. After it you can add a greeting such as 你好, or a question such as 是王老师吗？ (Is that Teacher Wang?).
In the course sentence, 喂 opens the call, 你好 greets the person, and 请问是哪位？ politely asks who is calling. 请问 means "may I ask", and 哪位 is a polite way to say "who".

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Nouns and numbers as predicates (no 是 needed)
structure: 时间 + 星期/日期/天气 noun
paragraphs: In Mandarin, a noun, pronoun, number phrase or noun phrase can act as the predicate by itself. You don't always need a verb like 是 (to be).
This is common when talking about the weather, the day, the date, time, age or price. For example: 今天晴天。 (It's sunny today.) 明天星期五。 (Tomorrow is Friday.)

To build it, put the topic first, then add the noun or number phrase directly after it. It sounds natural in short, simple statements. If you add 是 here, the meaning stays much the same, but it can sound more formal or emphatic.

edits.text: You can form result complements with 完 (wán). This indicates that an action is finished or completed.
If there is an object after the verb, 完 must be placed between the verb and the object. To indicate completion, 了 usually goes after the object.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Counting actions with 一下 and 一次
paragraphs: A number plus a measure word can come after a verb to say how many times, or for how long, an action happens. These are called action-measure complements.

The most common one for beginners is 一下(儿) after a verb. It means "a bit" or "one time", and makes a request or suggestion sound lighter and more casual: 等一下儿 is "wait a moment". You can also count real occurrences, like 去过一次 (have gone once).
Put the complement right after the verb: 介绍一下, 准备一下. Note that 一下(儿) is often used with 来 to mean "let me do something": 我来介绍一下.

edits.text: Although we have avoided 把 sentences so far for the sake of simplicity, you may have noticed that sentences which feature result complements often also use 把. This is because 把 sentences and result complements work particularly well together, as they both deal with the result of an action or the "disposal" of an object. Apart from result complements involving perception and psychological verbs, most result compounds work nicely in 把 sentences.
Given sufficient context, it's possible to use 多了 without the full comparison pattern. 多了 is the only one of the three "much more" phrases introduced here which can be used this way.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Sentences with a noun as the predicate
paragraphs: In Chinese, a noun phrase can sometimes follow the subject directly, with no 是 ("to be") between them.
This is common for simple facts such as weather, dates, time, age, nationality, and price: 明天阴天。(Tomorrow is cloudy.) 他中国人。(He is Chinese.)
To say "not", you must add 不是: 他不是中国人。 Adding 是 to a positive sentence is also correct. The version without 是 just sounds shorter and more casual.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Giving and telling with two objects (双宾语句)
structure: 我 + 给 + 妹妹 + 一本书
老师 + 教 + 我们 + 汉字
paragraphs: Some Chinese verbs can take two objects right after them. The first object is the person who receives something. The second is the thing given, taught, or told. This is called 双宾语句 (double-object sentence).

Use it with verbs about giving or passing on information, such as 给 (give), 教 (teach), and 告诉 (tell). The order is fixed: person first, then thing. In English we might say "give a book to my sister", but in Chinese you simply say 给妹妹一本书.
Adding 请 at the start makes a polite request, as in 请给我……

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Contrasting ideas with 但是 ("but")
paragraphs: A contrast sentence (转折复句) joins two clauses where the second goes against what you'd expect from the first. In English, this is "but" or "however."
Say your first idea, add a comma, then put 但 or 但是 at the start of the second clause. 但 is a shorter form of 但是. 可是 works in a similar way.

The first clause often gives a good point, and the second adds a problem. The official examples show this: 样子不错，有点儿贵 (looks nice, but a bit expensive). Sometimes the contrast word is left out, and the comma carries the meaning.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Direction complements: verb + 来/去
structure: Verb + 上 / 下 + (来 / 去)
paragraphs: A direction complement comes right after a verb and shows which way the action moves. 来 means toward the speaker. 去 means away from the speaker.
Words like 上 (up, onto) and 下 (down) can also follow a verb. They can combine with 来 or 去, as in 走下去 (go down, away from the speaker) and 下来 (come down, toward the speaker).
Repeating the pattern, as in 游来游去, describes movement back and forth.

edits.text: As you can see, when the verb is followed by an object, 的 can go before or after the object. Both sentences are grammatically correct, but the first sentence could be referring to either a specific event in the past or habitual actions.

It is also important to know that you can't use 了 in this type of sentence. 了 only tells you that the action is completed, not any of the other details that this construction is looking for. Since it is already understood that the action took place, the 了 is unhelpful and inappropriate.

Sometimes you can use 的 to really add a kick to your responses, making them stronger. You might even hear Chinese people reply with just 是的 which means "That's right." This usage is similar to the way that English speakers might stress the word "is" in sentences like "It is my food." When used to express affirmation, 会, 能, and 可以 are often used as well. The 是 is optional.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Choosing between options with 还是
structure: Subj. + Verb + A + 还是 + B?
你 + 坐火车，(还是) 坐飞机?
paragraphs: This pattern asks someone to choose between two or more options. In English it is like "Do you want A or B?"

Put 还是 ("or") between the options: A 还是 B? You can repeat the verb in the second part, as in 喝茶. Do not add 吗 to this kind of question. Casual speech sometimes drops 还是 and just says the two options one after the other.
In the example, the speaker asks a question and then offers a second choice with 还是: eat something, or drink tea?

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Two actions in a row (serial verbs)
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Vehicle + 去 + Place
paragraphs: Chinese can put two verb phrases side by side with no word for "and" or "then" between them. The verbs come in the order the actions happen, and the subject is said only once.
A very common pattern starts with 去 (go) plus a place, then says what you do there: 去药店买药 means go to the pharmacy, then buy medicine.
You can also start with 坐 plus a vehicle, then 去: 坐地铁去上班. Just keep the verbs in the order they happen.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Ongoing states with verb + 着
paragraphs: Put 着 after a verb to show that an action or state is continuing. It describes how things are now, as in 灯亮着 (The light is on) or 电脑开着 (The computer is on).
To negate it, use 没 before the verb: 灯没亮着. The 着 can stay.
着 also links two actions. The first verb with 着 shows the manner or state in which the second action happens. In 他在门口笑着看我, 笑着 (smiling) describes how he looks at me (看我).

edits.text: The questions could be asking about current possession ("Do you have it or not?"), or to ask about verbs in the past ("Did you do it or not?").

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Asking to confirm with 吧
paragraphs: Add 吧 to the end of a statement to turn it into a question. You are not asking for new information. You already have a guess, and you want the other person to confirm it. It is similar to "..., right?" or "I guess you...?" in English.

To build it, say your guess as a normal statement, then put 吧 at the end and use a question mark. You do not need 吗. For example, 您是经理吧？ means "You're the manager, right?" and 你以前学过中文吧？ means "You've studied Chinese before, right?"
Use it when you feel fairly sure of the answer. If you have no idea, 吗 is the better choice.

[\"tip\", 1, \"claude-sonnet-5-5\", \"2-.title: Expressing past experience with 过
structure: Subj. + 没(有) + Verb + 过 + Object
paragraphs: Put 过 right after a verb to say someone has done something before, at least once. It talks about life experience, not a single event at a specific time.
In 我见过这个人, 见过 means “have seen”. In 我去过那里多次, 多次 (“many times”) is added after the object to say how often.
To say you have never done something, put 没(有) before the verb and keep 过: 我没去过那里. To ask, add 吗: 你去过那里吗?

tips.title: 能
tips.meaning: 能 means can: someone is able to do something, or it is possible or allowed.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 会
tips.meaning: 会 means can: someone knows how to do something they have learned, like a language or cooking.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English 'can' is one word, but Chinese 会 fits learned skills best.

tips.title: 想
tips.meaning: 想 means want to, or would like to, do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
structure: Subj. + 不 + 想 + Verb (+ Obj.)

tips.title: 要
tips.meaning: 要 means want something or want to do something; it can also mean will or need to.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb or noun you want.

tips.title: Number + Measure word + Noun
tips.meaning: Number words say how many of something there are.
tips.placement: Put the number right before the measure word, and the noun comes after.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 这 / 那
tips.meaning: 这 means "this" and 那 means "that".
tips.placement: Put it first, before a noun, or use it alone with 是.
tips.english_note: Before a noun, Chinese needs a measure word in between, and 个 is a good one to start with.
structure: 这 / 那 + Measure Word + Noun

tips.title: 这些 / 那些
tips.meaning: 这些 means "these" and 那些 means "those", for more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it before a noun, or use it alone.

tips.title: 这里 / 这儿
tips.meaning: 这里 and 这儿 both mean "here".
tips.placement: It often comes at the start of the sentence.
structure: 这里 / 这儿 + 有 / 没有 + Noun

tips.title: 那里 / 那儿
tips.meaning: 那里 and 那儿 both mean "there".
tips.placement: It often comes at the start of the sentence.
structure: 那里 / 那儿 + 有 / 没有 + Noun

tips.title: 个
tips.meaning: 个 is the most common measure word, used for people and many everyday things.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word after a number, but English just uses the noun.

tips.title: 杯
tips.meaning: 杯 counts cups or glasses of a drink.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the drink.
tips.english_note: It works like "a cup of", but Chinese needs no word for "of".

tips.title: 本
tips.meaning: 本 counts books.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the book.

tips.title: 家
tips.meaning: 家 counts shops, restaurants and companies.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the noun.

tips.title: 间
tips.meaning: 间 counts rooms.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the noun.

tips.title: 口
tips.meaning: 口 counts the people in a family.
tips.placement: Put it after the number, before 人.

tips.title: 块
tips.meaning: 块 means yuan, the unit of money, in everyday speech.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number of yuan.
tips.english_note: It comes after the number, but English puts the money sign before it.

tips.title: 页
tips.meaning: 页 counts pages.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the noun.

tips.title: 非常
tips.meaning: 非常 means "very" or "extremely".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, or before a verb like 喜欢.
structure: Subj. + 非常 + 喜欢 + Obj.

tips.title: 很
tips.meaning: 很 links a subject to an adjective, and it can also mean "very".
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.
tips.english_note: Where English says "is" before an adjective, Chinese uses 很, not 是.

tips.title: 太
tips.meaning: 太 means "too" or "so", and it often shows a strong feeling.
tips.placement: Put 太 before the adjective and 了 after it.

tips.title: 真
tips.meaning: 真 means "really" or "so", and it shows a strong feeling.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.

tips.title: 最
tips.meaning: 最 means "the most".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, or before 喜欢 to say what you like best.
tips.english_note: Chinese always uses 最 for "-est", so there is no special form to learn.

tips.title: 我 / 我们
tips.meaning: 我 means I or me, and 我们 means we or us.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to mean "my".
tips.english_note: The same word is used for I and me.

tips.title: 你 / 你们
tips.meaning: 你 means you for one person, and 你们 means you for two or more people.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to mean "your".
tips.english_note: The same word is used for subject and object, and 你们 is a separate word for a group.

tips.title: 您
tips.meaning: 您 is a polite way to say you to one person.
tips.placement: Use it in the same places as 你.
tips.english_note: English has no polite you.

tips.title: 他 / 他们
tips.meaning: 他 means he or him, and 他们 means they or them.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to mean "his".
tips.english_note: The same word is used for he and him.

tips.title: 她 / 她们
tips.meaning: 她 means she or her, and 她们 means they or them for women or girls.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to mean "her".
tips.english_note: The same word is used for she and her.

tips.title: 都
tips.meaning: 都 means "all" or "both" for the people or things you are talking about.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English "all" can start a sentence, but 都 never goes first.

tips.title: 一起
tips.meaning: 一起 means doing something together with other people.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "together" after the verb, but 一起 comes before it.

tips.title: 一块儿
tips.meaning: 一块儿 means doing something together, just like 一起.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "together" after the verb, but 一块儿 comes before it.

tips.title: 马上
tips.meaning: 马上 means something will happen right away or very soon.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 先
tips.meaning: 先 means to do something first, before doing other things.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 有时
tips.meaning: 有时 means sometimes.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 在 / 正在 / 正
tips.meaning: These show that an action is happening right now. 正在 stresses the "right now" a little more.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts a word before the verb, not -ing after it.
structure: Subj. + 在 / 正在 / 正 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 从
tips.meaning: 从 means "from" and tells where or when something starts.
tips.placement: Put it before the place or time, and before the verb.
tips.english_note: In English "from" often comes after the verb, but 从 comes before it.

tips.title: 比
tips.meaning: 比 means "than". It compares two things, and the first one comes out higher.
tips.english_note: In English "than" comes after the adjective, but 比 goes before it, between the two things.

tips.title: 也
tips.meaning: 也 means "also" or "too" and shows someone else does the same thing.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, before the verb.
tips.english_note: English can say "too" at the end, but 也 never goes at the end.

tips.title: 还
tips.meaning: 还 adds one more thing, like "and also" or "what else".
tips.placement: Put it before the verb of the extra thing.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., 还 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 在
tips.meaning: 在 means "at", "in" or "on" and shows where someone or something is, or where an action happens.
tips.placement: To say where you do something, put 在 and the place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the place after the verb, but Chinese puts it before.

tips.title: 常常 / 常
tips.meaning: 常常 means "often", and 常 means the same thing.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English can say "often" at the end, but Chinese puts it before the verb.

tips.title: 再
tips.meaning: 再 means you will do something again, or do some more of it, later.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "again" at the end, but 再 comes before the verb.

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use it to join things or people, not to join two actions.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "with" someone.
tips.placement: Put 跟 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "with" after the verb, but Chinese puts it before.

tips.title: Verb sentence
tips.meaning: A verb tells what the subject does, and an object can follow the verb to say what it acts on.
tips.placement: Put the verb right after the subject, and the object right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Word order is the same as in English: who, does, what.

tips.title: Verb + 了
tips.meaning: 了 shows that an action is finished.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, or at the end of the sentence when the object is short.
tips.english_note: English changes the verb (bought); Chinese keeps the verb and adds 了.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Obj.

tips.title: Number + Measure word
tips.meaning: A number plus a measure word tells how many of something there are.
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun it counts, usually after the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun, a bit like "a cup of" tea.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 不
tips.meaning: 不 means "not" and makes a verb or adjective negative.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or adjective.

tips.title: 没(有)
tips.meaning: 没(有) says that something did not happen, or that you do not have something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or noun.

tips.title: 别
tips.meaning: 别 means "don't" and tells someone not to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: An adjective can describe the subject directly, like 'is small' or 'is good'.
tips.placement: Put the adjective right after the subject, often with 很 or another word like 非常 or 太 before it.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word for 'is' before the adjective.

tips.title: 还是
tips.meaning: 还是 means "or" when you ask someone to pick one of two choices.
tips.placement: Put it between the two choices in a question.
tips.english_note: Use it only in questions, not for "or" in statements.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Noun + 还是 + Noun ?

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use it only for nouns, not to join two verbs.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.

tips.title: 的
tips.meaning: 的 shows that something belongs to someone, like 's in English.
tips.placement: Put it between the owner and the thing owned.
tips.english_note: 我的 simply means "my", and 谁的 means "whose".

tips.title: 地
tips.meaning: 地 links a word that says how someone does something to the verb.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: It works a bit like "-ly" in English, such as "quietly".

tips.title: Basic statement: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: This is the plain way to say something: who does what, or what something is like.
tips.english_note: Chinese keeps the same order as English, and to say no, you put 不 right before the verb.

tips.title: 是
tips.meaning: 是 links two nouns, like "is", "am" or "are".
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns, after the subject.
tips.english_note: 是 links nouns only, so don't use it before an adjective, and it never changes for I, you or he.

tips.title: A 比 B + Adj.
tips.meaning: This compares two things: A is more of something than B.
tips.placement: Put 比 and the thing you compare with between the subject and the adjective.
tips.english_note: English adds -er or 'more' to the adjective; Chinese keeps the adjective plain and puts 比 before it.

tips.title: Two short sentences side by side
tips.meaning: Put two short sentences next to each other to compare or list two things.
tips.placement: Join them with a comma and no linking word; the second sentence often mirrors the first.
tips.english_note: English often adds 'and' or 'but'; Chinese just uses a comma.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., Subj. + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: Sentences with no subject
tips.meaning: Some sentences are just one word or a short phrase, with no subject, to call out, greet, or say what is happening.
tips.placement: Say it alone as a full sentence; you don't need to add a subject.
tips.english_note: English often adds "it" or "I", but Chinese doesn't need one here.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as a statement; English changes the order.

tips.title: 了
tips.meaning: 了 shows that something has happened or has become different.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a sentence a soft suggestion or request.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: 呢
tips.meaning: 呢 asks "and what about...?" to ask the same question back.
tips.placement: Put it right after a noun or a person word like 你.

tips.title: Sentence + 了
tips.meaning: Shows that something has changed, so it is new or different now.
tips.placement: Put 了 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English says "now", "became" or "anymore", but Chinese just adds 了.

tips.title: 请 + Verb
tips.meaning: 请 means "please" and makes a polite request or invitation.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence, before the verb.

tips.title: 别 + Verb
tips.meaning: 别 means "don't" and tells someone not to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: Verb + Obj. (command)
tips.meaning: To tell someone to do something, start with the verb and leave out 你. Adding 吧 at the end makes it softer.

tips.title: 有
tips.meaning: 有 means to have, or that something is in a place.
tips.placement: Put it between the person or place and the thing.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 有 for both "have" and "there is."

tips.title: 没有
tips.meaning: 没有 means do not have, or there is none.
tips.english_note: To say "don't have," use 没有, never 不有.

tips.title: Exclamations (！)
tips.meaning: Shows strong feeling, like surprise or delight, about how something is.
tips.placement: Put 太 or 真 before the adjective, add 了 after the adjective when you use 太, and end with ！

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: Word order stays the same as the statement; just add 吗 at the end.

tips.title: 在 + Verb
tips.meaning: 在 shows that an action is happening right now.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no -ing ending, so 在 does that job.

tips.title: 正在 + Verb
tips.meaning: 正在 shows that an action is happening right at this moment.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 正 + Verb
tips.meaning: 正 is a short form of 正在, and it also shows an action is happening right now.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
structure: Subj. + 正 + Verb + Obj. (+ 呢)

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement; English changes the order or adds "do".

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who" and asks about a person.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like "who" often does in English.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what" and asks about a thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like "what" does in English.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks about a small number, such as the hour.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word or a time word like 点.
tips.english_note: To ask the time, Chinese says "几点" for "what time".

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which" and asks you to pick one from several.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like "which" does in English.

tips.title: 怎么了
tips.meaning: 怎么了 asks "What's wrong?" or "What happened?"
tips.placement: Put it after the person you are asking about.

tips.title: 还是
tips.meaning: Means "or" in a question, and asks the listener to pick one of two choices.
tips.placement: Put it between the two choices.
tips.english_note: English can use "or" anywhere, but 还是 is for questions.
structure: Option A + 还是 + Option B?
Subj. + Verb + Option A + 还是 + Option B?

tips.title: Verb + 了
tips.meaning: 了 after a verb shows that an action happened or was completed.
tips.placement: Put 了 right after the verb, before the number and noun.
tips.english_note: The Chinese verb never changes form; you add 了 instead.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Obj.

tips.title: Verb/Adj. + 不/没 + Verb/Adj.?
tips.meaning: Say a verb or adjective, then its negative, to ask a yes-or-no question.
tips.placement: Put it where the verb or adjective would normally go.
tips.english_note: English adds 'or not' at the end; Chinese puts the two choices side by side.

tips.title: 多少钱
tips.meaning: This question asks the price of something.
tips.placement: Say the thing first and put 多少钱 at the end.
tips.english_note: The question words stay at the end, so nothing moves to the front like "How much" does in English.

tips.title: 块 / 元
tips.meaning: 块 is the everyday word for the main unit of Chinese money, like "yuan" or "bucks". 元 means the same and is more formal.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number; 钱 can come after it.
tips.english_note: The money word goes after the number, not before it like a $ sign.

tips.title: 毛
tips.meaning: 毛 is a smaller unit of money, one tenth of a 块.
tips.placement: Put it after the number that comes after 块. You can leave 毛 off at the end.

tips.title: 可能
tips.meaning: 可能 means something may be true or may happen, and 不可能 means it is not possible.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 千
tips.meaning: 千 means thousand. Put a number before it to count thousands.

tips.title: 万
tips.meaning: 万 means ten thousand, so 一万 is 10,000 and 两万 is 20,000.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, then the measure word and noun.
tips.english_note: English has no single word for ten thousand, so think of big numbers in groups of four digits.

tips.title: 亿
tips.meaning: 亿 means hundred million, so 一亿 is 100,000,000.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, then the measure word and noun.
tips.english_note: English has no single word for hundred million.

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: This means morning, or a.m.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.

tips.title: 下午
tips.meaning: This means afternoon, or p.m.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.

tips.title: 晚上
tips.meaning: This means evening or night.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: This means o'clock. Use 几点 to ask what time it is.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number of the hour.
tips.english_note: The time usually goes before the verb, not at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: 分
tips.meaning: This means minutes.
tips.placement: Put it after the number of minutes, which comes after 点.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: This word means week. With a number, it names a day of the week.

tips.title: 年
tips.meaning: This means year.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number of the year. It comes first in a full date.
tips.english_note: Dates go from big to small: year, month, day.
structure: Number + 年 + Number + 月 + Number + 号

tips.title: 月
tips.meaning: This means month. The number comes before it.
tips.placement: Put it after the year and before the day.

tips.title: 号
tips.meaning: This means the day of the month. People use it a lot when speaking.
tips.placement: Put it after the number of the day, at the end of the date.

tips.title: 这么 / 那么
tips.meaning: Both mean "so" before an adjective; 这么 points to something near, 那么 to something far.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.
structure: Subj. + 这么 / 那么 + Adj.

tips.title: 这样 / 那样
tips.meaning: 这样 means "this way" and 那样 means "that way".
tips.placement: Put it before the verb it describes.
tips.english_note: English usually says "this way" after the verb, but Chinese puts it before.

tips.title: 多久
tips.meaning: 多久 asks how long something takes or lasts.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb.
tips.english_note: English starts with "how long", but 多久 comes later in the sentence.

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 asks why.
tips.placement: Put it right after the subject, before the verb.
tips.english_note: English "why" starts the question, but 为什么 usually follows the subject.

tips.title: 怎么样 / 怎样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the question, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: You don't need a word for "is".
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样?

tips.title: Verb + Verb
tips.meaning: Saying a verb twice means doing it a little or for a short time, in a casual way.
tips.placement: Put both copies where the verb normally goes; with a two-character verb, repeat the whole verb.
tips.english_note: English adds 'a little' or 'a bit', but Chinese just repeats the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 一 + Verb
tips.meaning: Putting 一 between two copies of a verb also means doing it a little or for a short time.

tips.title: 别人
tips.meaning: 别人 means other people, not you and not me.
tips.placement: Put it where you would put a noun, such as the subject or the object.
tips.english_note: English needs two words, "other people", but Chinese uses just one.

tips.title: 大家
tips.meaning: 大家 means everyone in the group.
tips.placement: Put it at the start as the subject, or right before a greeting like 好.

tips.title: 它 / 它们
tips.meaning: 它 means "it" for an animal or thing, and 它们 means "they" for animals or things.
tips.placement: Put it where you would put a subject.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses a different word for people, not 它.

tips.title: 咱们 / 咱
tips.meaning: 咱们 means "we", and it always includes the person you are talking to.
tips.placement: Put it where you would put a subject.
tips.english_note: English "we" may or may not include the listener, but 咱们 always does.

tips.title: 自己
tips.meaning: 自己 means yourself, myself, himself and so on, pointing back to the person doing the action.
tips.placement: Put it right after a person word, or after a verb as the object.
tips.english_note: One word 自己 covers myself, yourself, himself and more.

tips.title: 层
tips.meaning: 层 is a measure word for floors (levels) of a building.
tips.placement: Put it right after a number.
tips.english_note: English says "three floors" the same way, but Chinese often needs the measure word with a number before a noun.

tips.title: 封
tips.meaning: 封 is a measure word for letters.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a letter"; Chinese adds 封 after the number.

tips.title: 件
tips.meaning: 件 is a measure word for clothes like shirts and coats, and also for matters (事).
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a coat"; Chinese adds 件 after the number.

tips.title: 条
tips.meaning: 条 is a measure word for long, thin things like pants, roads, rivers and fish.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a road"; Chinese adds 条 after the number.

tips.title: 位
tips.meaning: 位 is a polite measure word for people.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "two teachers"; Chinese adds 位 after the number.

tips.title: 分钟
tips.meaning: 分钟 means "minutes" and tells how long an action lasted.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb, with the number before it and the object after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for" here; the time just follows the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 分钟 + Obj.

tips.title: 年
tips.meaning: 年 means "years" and tells how long an action lasted.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb, with the number before it and the object after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for" here; the time just follows the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 年 + Obj.

tips.title: 天
tips.meaning: 天 means "days" and tells how long an action lasted.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb, with the number before it and the object after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for" here; the time just follows the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 天 + Obj.

tips.title: 周
tips.meaning: 周 means "weeks" and tells how long an action lasted.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb, with the number before it and the object after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for" here; the time just follows the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 周 + Obj.

tips.title: 往
tips.meaning: 往 means "toward" and shows which direction you do something in.
tips.placement: Put 往 and the direction or place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the verb first ("go left"); Chinese puts 往 + direction before the verb.

tips.title: 全 / 全都
tips.meaning: 全 means all or everyone, with none left out.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, before the verb.

tips.title: 一共
tips.meaning: 一共 means "in total" or "altogether" when you add things up.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, before the number.
structure: Subj. + 一共 + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 只
tips.meaning: 只 means "only" or "just".
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 给
tips.meaning: 给 shows who an action is for or aimed at, like "to" or "for" someone.
tips.placement: Put 给 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the person after the verb ("call him"), but Chinese puts 给 + person before it.

tips.title: 次
tips.meaning: 次 counts how many times you do something, like "times" in English.
tips.placement: Put the number and 次 right after the verb.

tips.title: 遍
tips.meaning: 遍 also counts how many times you do something, like saying or reading something again.
tips.placement: Put the number and 遍 right after the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 一下
tips.meaning: 一下 makes an action short and light, like "a little bit", and can make it sound softer.
tips.placement: Put 一下 right after the verb.

tips.title: 已经
tips.meaning: 已经 means "already": something is done or has become true.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, and usually add 了 at the end.

tips.title: 一直
tips.meaning: 一直 means something keeps going all the time, "always" or "all along".
tips.placement: Put it before the verb or adjective.

tips.title: 刚 / 刚刚
tips.meaning: 刚 and 刚刚 mean "just": something happened a moment ago. They mean the same thing.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 就
tips.meaning: Means "then": the first part gives a situation, and the part with 就 says the result.
tips.placement: Put 就 in the second part, right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English "then" can start the part, but 就 stays before the verb.
structure: 如果 + Situation, Subj. + 就 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 离
tips.meaning: 离 tells how far or close one place is from another place.
tips.placement: Put 离 between the two places, then add 近 or 远 after the second place.
tips.english_note: English puts "from" after "far", but Chinese puts 离 and the second place before 远 or 近.
structure: Place 1 + 离 + Place 2 + (很) + 近 / 远

tips.title: 从
tips.meaning: 从 means "from" and shows the place where something starts.
tips.placement: Put 从 and the place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "from" after the verb, but Chinese puts 从 + place before it.

tips.title: Verb + 得
tips.meaning: 得 links an action to a comment on how well or how it was done.
tips.placement: Put 得 right after the verb, then add the comment, like 很好.
tips.english_note: English says "slept well"; Chinese puts 得 between the verb and the comment.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 得 + 很 + Adj.
Subj. + Obj. + Verb + 得 + 很 + Adj.

tips.title: 重新
tips.meaning: 重新 means to do something again from the beginning.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 经常
tips.meaning: 经常 means "often".
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.

tips.title: 老(是)
tips.meaning: 老是 means "always", and it often sounds like a complaint.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.

tips.title: 又
tips.meaning: 又 means something happened again.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, and 了 often comes at the end.
tips.english_note: English puts "again" at the end, but 又 goes before the verb.
structure: Subj. + 又 + 不 / 没 + Verb

tips.title: 对
tips.meaning: 对 shows who or what an action or feeling is aimed at, like "to," "at," "toward" or "about."
tips.placement: Put 对 and the person or thing right after the subject, before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English says "to" or "at" after the verb, but Chinese puts 对 + person before it.

tips.title: Verb + 过
tips.meaning: 过 says you have done something at least once before, so it talks about experience.
tips.placement: Put 过 right after the verb; to say you never have, put 没 before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word for "ever" or "before"; 过 does that job.
structure: Subj. + 没 + Verb + 过 + Obj.

tips.title: 有(一)点(儿)
tips.meaning: It means "a little too" and is usually used for things you don't like.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 挺
tips.meaning: It means "quite" or "pretty", as in "pretty good".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, and 的 often comes at the end.

tips.title: 更
tips.meaning: It means "even more".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 更 before the adjective instead of adding "-er" to it.

tips.title: 特别
tips.meaning: It means "especially" or "very".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 十分
tips.meaning: It means "very".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 多么
tips.meaning: It means "how...!" and shows strong feeling.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, and 啊 often comes at the end.
tips.english_note: It works like "how" in "How pretty!"

tips.title: 喂
tips.meaning: Say 喂 to greet someone when you answer or make a phone call, like "hello".
tips.placement: Put it at the very start, then add what you want to say.
tips.english_note: English "hello" is for any greeting, but 喂 is mostly used on the phone.

tips.title: 什么的
tips.meaning: It means "and so on" and ends a list of things, in a casual way.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of a list of two or three items.
tips.english_note: English puts "and so on" after the last item too, but Chinese has no "and" before the last item.

tips.title: Verb + 着
tips.meaning: 着 shows a state that keeps going, like a door that is closed, or someone smiling while they do something else.
tips.placement: Put 着 right after the verb; if another verb follows, it is the main action.

tips.title: 还是……吧
tips.meaning: This suggests the better choice, like "we'd better" or "let's", often after thinking about other options.
tips.placement: Put 还是 before the verb and 吧 at the end.
structure: Subj. + 还是 + Verb + Obj. + 吧

tips.title: Noun or number as the whole description
tips.meaning: A noun, or a number with a measure word, can describe the subject all by itself, with no verb.
tips.placement: Put it right after the subject.
tips.english_note: English needs "is" here, but Chinese usually leaves out 是.

tips.title: Noun as the sentence's main statement
tips.meaning: A noun can tell the time, weather, origin or age of the subject, with no verb like 是.
tips.english_note: English needs 'is' here, but Chinese often leaves out 是 when saying these things.

tips.title: Verb + 来/去 (direction)
tips.meaning: A direction word after a verb shows which way the action moves.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb; 上, 下, 进, 出, 回, 过 or 起 can come before 来 or 去.
tips.english_note: 来 means moving toward the speaker, and 去 means moving away.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 上/下/进/出/回/过/起 + 来/去

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a sentence softer and friendlier, like a gentle suggestion: "let's..." or "how about...".
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English uses "let's" or a gentle tone; Chinese just adds 吧 at the end.

tips.title: 啊
tips.meaning: After each item in a list, 啊 sounds casual, as if saying "and things like that".
tips.placement: Put it right after each noun in the list.
structure: Noun + 啊, Noun + 啊, Noun + 啊, ……

tips.title: Place + Verb + 着 + Noun
tips.meaning: Says that something or someone is standing, sitting, lying or placed somewhere.
tips.placement: Start with the place, then the verb with 着, then what is there.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts the place first and the thing last, like 'On the desk lies a book'.
structure: Place + Verb + 着 + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: Verb + Verb (two actions in order)
tips.meaning: Two actions in a row: the first happens, then the second.
tips.placement: Put the verbs one after the other, in the order they happen, with no extra word between them.
tips.english_note: English often adds "and" or "to" between the actions; Chinese just puts the verbs side by side.
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Noun + 去 + Place

tips.title: Verb + 完
tips.meaning: 完 shows that you finished doing the action.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, before any object.
tips.english_note: English says "finish the movie", but Chinese needs the action verb before 完.
structure: Subj. + 没 + Verb + 完 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 错
tips.meaning: 错 shows that you did the action wrongly and made a mistake.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 错 after the verb where English uses "wrongly".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 错 + 了 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 好
tips.meaning: 好 shows that the action was done well or is completely finished.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 好 + 了 + Obj.
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 好 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 懂
tips.meaning: 懂 shows that you understood what you read, heard or studied.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 懂 + 了 + Obj.
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 懂 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 会
tips.meaning: 会 shows that after doing the action, you now know how to do it.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 会 + 了 + Obj.
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 会 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 清楚
tips.meaning: 清楚 shows that you saw, heard or understood something clearly.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 清楚 after the verb where English uses "clearly".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 清楚 + 了 + Obj.
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 清楚 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 干净
tips.meaning: 干净 shows that the action made something clean.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 干净 + 了 + Obj.
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 干净 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + person + thing (double object)
tips.meaning: Some verbs like 给, 教 and 告诉 can take two objects: first the person, then the thing.
tips.placement: Put the person right after the verb, and the thing after the person.
tips.english_note: Unlike English, there is no word like "to" between the verb and the person.
structure: Subj. + 给 + Obj. (person) + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: Shows an action is quick or short, and makes it sound softer and more casual.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, before any object.

tips.title: Verb + Number + 次
tips.meaning: Tells how many times an action happens.
tips.placement: Put the number and 次 right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "times" later in the sentence, but Chinese puts it straight after the verb.

tips.title: A 比 B + Adj.
tips.meaning: 比 means "than" and shows that the first thing has more of a quality than the second.
tips.placement: Put 比 between the two things you compare, and put the adjective at the end.
tips.english_note: English says the adjective before "than", but Chinese puts it after the second thing.

tips.title: Adj. + 一点(儿) / 一些
tips.meaning: It means "a little more" or "a bit more" than before or than something else.
tips.placement: Put it right after the adjective.
tips.english_note: English puts "a bit" or "a little" before the adjective, but Chinese puts it after.

tips.title: Adj. + 得多 / 多了
tips.meaning: It means "much more" than something else or than before.
tips.placement: Put it right after the adjective.
tips.english_note: English puts "much" before the adjective, but Chinese puts it after.
structure: A + 比 + B + Adj. + 得多

tips.title: 大 / 小 + Number + 岁
tips.meaning: It tells how many years older or younger one person is than another.
tips.placement: Put 大 or 小 first, then the number, then 岁.
tips.english_note: English says the number first and then "older", but Chinese says 大 or 小 first.
structure: A + 比 + B + 大 / 小 + Number + 岁

tips.title: 是……的
tips.meaning: It points out a detail, like when, where or how, of something that already happened.
tips.placement: Put 是 before the detail and 的 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English stresses the detail with your voice or says "it was... that".
structure: Subj. + 是 + Time + Verb + 的
Subj. + 是 + 在 + Place + Verb + 的

tips.title: 有 (as … as)
tips.meaning: 有 says something reaches an amount, or is as much as something else.
tips.placement: Put 有 after the subject, then the amount or the other person or thing, then the adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese says "has" where English says "is as tall as".
structure: Subj. + 有 + Number + Measure word + Adj.
Subj. + 有 + Noun + Adj. + 吗?

tips.title: Verb + 着
tips.meaning: 着 shows that an action or state keeps going on, like something that stays in place: 灯亮着 means the light is on.
tips.placement: Put 着 right after the verb.

tips.title: 第
tips.meaning: Put 第 before a number to make it 'first', 'second', 'third' and so on.
tips.placement: Put it right before the number, then add a measure word and noun if you need one.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 第 for every number, so there is no -st, -nd, -rd or -th to learn.

tips.title: A 还是 B
tips.meaning: This asks someone to choose between two options, like "A or B?"
tips.placement: Put 还是 between the two choices.
structure: Subj. + Verb + A + 还是 + B?
Subj. + Verb + A + 还是 + Verb + B?

tips.title: 一……就……
tips.meaning: It means "as soon as" the first thing happens, the second thing happens right after (or happens every time).
tips.placement: Put 一 before the first verb and 就 before the second verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses both 一 and 就, where English only says "as soon as".
structure: Subj. + 一 + Verb (+ Obj.) + 就 + Verb (+ Obj.)
一 + Verb (+ Obj.), Subj. + 就 + Verb (+ Obj.)

tips.title: Verb + 过
tips.meaning: Shows that someone has done something before, at some time in the past.
tips.placement: Put 过 right after the verb; to say you never have, put 没 before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "have" here; 过 after the verb does that job.
structure: Subj. + 没 + Verb + 过 + Obj.

tips.title: Noun + 呢？
tips.meaning: Asks "what about...?" or "how about...?" after something was just said, and can also ask where someone or something is.
tips.placement: Put 呢 at the end, right after the person or thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no verb here; the noun plus 呢 is the whole question.

tips.title: 因为
tips.meaning: 因为 introduces the reason and means "because".
tips.placement: Put it right before the reason, usually at the start of the sentence or after the result.
structure: 因为 + reason, 所以 + result

tips.title: 所以
tips.meaning: 所以 introduces the result and means "so".
tips.placement: Put it right before the result, after the reason.
tips.english_note: Chinese can use 因为 and 所以 in the same sentence, but English uses only one of "because" and "so".
structure: 因为 + reason, 所以 + result

tips.title: 但是 / 但
tips.meaning: Means "but": the second part says something that goes against the first part.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the second part, after a comma.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., 但是 + Subj. + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 就 / 就是
tips.meaning: 就 adds emphasis, like "exactly" or "right", to say that something is just so.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb, most often 是 or 在.

tips.title: Number + 多
tips.meaning: 多 after a number means "more than" that number.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number, before the measure word.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts "more than" after the number, not before it.

tips.title: 几 + Measure word
tips.meaning: 几 means "a few" or "several", a small number you don't say exactly.
tips.placement: Use it where a number would go, before the measure word.

tips.title: Number + 左右
tips.meaning: 左右 means "about" or "around" an amount.
tips.placement: Put it after the number and measure word.
tips.english_note: Chinese says "about" after the amount, not before it.

tips.title: 好吗
tips.meaning: Asks if the other person agrees with your suggestion or request, like "OK?" in English.
tips.placement: Say your suggestion first, then add 好吗 at the end.

tips.title: 可以吗
tips.meaning: Asks if something is okay or allowed, like "Is that OK?" or "May I?"
tips.placement: Say your idea first, then add 可以吗 at the end.

tips.title: 行吗
tips.meaning: Asks if something is okay with the other person, like "Is that OK?"
tips.placement: Say your idea first, then add 行吗 at the end.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: English puts "how" first, but 怎么样 comes at the end.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样？

tips.title: 是不是
tips.meaning: It asks "is it so or not?" to check whether something is true.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, or at the start of the sentence you want to check.
tips.english_note: Chinese keeps the normal word order and just adds 是不是, so the sentence is not turned around like English "Is he...?"

tips.title: Sentence + 吧？
tips.meaning: Ending a sentence with 吧 makes it a question where you already guess the answer and want the other person to confirm.
tips.placement: Put 吧 at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: It works like adding "right?" at the end in English.

tips.title: 快要……了
tips.meaning: 快要 means something is about to happen very soon.
tips.placement: Put 快要 before the verb and 了 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs 了 at the end, but English has no matching word.

tips.title: 就要……了
tips.meaning: 就要 means something is about to happen, and it can follow a time like 下个月.
tips.placement: Put 就要 before the verb and 了 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs 了 at the end, but English has no matching word.

tips.title: 要……了
tips.meaning: 要 with 了 means something is about to happen.
tips.placement: Put 要 before the verb and 了 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs 了 at the end, but English has no matching word.

tips.title: 什么时候
tips.meaning: Asks "when", to find out the time of something.
tips.placement: Put it where the time word would go, usually after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "when" first, but Chinese keeps it in the middle of the sentence.
structure: Subj. + 什么时候 + Verb + Obj.?

tips.title: 什么样
tips.meaning: Asks "what kind of", to find out what something or someone is like.
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun you are asking about, usually with 的.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么样的 + Noun?

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: Asks "why", to find out the reason for something.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "why" first, but Chinese puts it after the subject.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like. It can also ask for an opinion.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the question, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English says "how is" first, but Chinese says the topic first.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样?

tips.title: 怎样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the question, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English says "how is" first, but Chinese says the topic first.

tips.title: 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪儿 means "where" and asks about a place.
tips.placement: Put it in the spot where the place would be in the answer.
tips.english_note: English moves "where" to the front, but Chinese keeps the normal word order.

tips.title: 玩儿
tips.meaning: 玩儿 means to play or to have fun.

tips.title: 一会儿
tips.meaning: 一会儿 means a short time, a little while.
tips.placement: Put it right after a verb to say how long.

tips.title: Basic statement
tips.meaning: A basic statement tells who does what, or what something is like.
tips.placement: Put the subject first, then the verb or adjective, then the object.

tips.title: Two short sentences side by side
tips.meaning: Two short sentences sit side by side to give two facts that go together or contrast.
tips.placement: Put them one after the other, with a comma between.
tips.english_note: English often adds a word like 'and' or 'but'; Chinese can simply put the two sentences next to each other.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., Subj. + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: Verb/Adj. + 不/没 + Verb/Adj.?
tips.meaning: This makes a yes-or-no question by putting a verb or adjective and its negative side by side.
tips.english_note: English adds 'or not'; Chinese repeats the verb or adjective with 不 or 没 instead.

tips.title: Sentences with no subject
tips.meaning: Some short sentences are just a word or phrase, with no subject, and still make complete sense.
tips.placement: Use them alone to call out, greet someone, or say what is happening.
tips.english_note: English often adds "it" (it's raining), but Chinese doesn't need it.

tips.title: 就
tips.meaning: 就 means "then": the first part gives a situation, and the second part says what follows from it.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, right before the verb in the second part.
tips.english_note: English often leaves out "then", but Chinese often keeps 就.

tips.title: 多少钱
tips.meaning: 多少钱 asks the price: how much money is it?
tips.placement: Put it after the thing you are asking about.

tips.title: 块 / 元
tips.meaning: 块 is the basic unit of money, like yuan. 元 means the same but sounds more formal.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number, and 钱 can come last.

tips.title: 毛
tips.meaning: 毛 is a small unit of money, one tenth of a 块.
tips.placement: Put it after the second number, which follows 块, and you can often leave 毛 off.

tips.title: 什么的
tips.meaning: It means "and so on" or "and things like that". It is casual, and it ends a list of things.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of a list of two or three nouns or actions.
structure: Verb + Obj., Verb + Obj. + 什么的

tips.title: 已经
tips.meaning: It means something has already happened or is already true.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, and add 了 at the end.

tips.title: 一直
tips.meaning: It means something keeps going all the time, without stopping.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb or adjective.

tips.title: 刚 / 刚刚
tips.meaning: It means something happened just a moment ago.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 忽然
tips.meaning: It means something happens suddenly, when you did not expect it.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: Noun/number as the description
tips.meaning: A noun, number or number + measure word can describe the subject by itself, with no 是 needed. It is common for time, date, weather and price.
tips.english_note: English needs 'is', but Chinese often leaves out 是 here.

tips.title: 对
tips.meaning: 对 shows who or what an action or feeling is aimed at.
tips.placement: Put 对 and the person or thing after the subject, before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English uses different words like "to," "at," or "about," but Chinese uses 对.

tips.title: Verb + Verb
tips.meaning: Say a verb twice to mean you do it a little or for a short time, in a casual way.
tips.placement: Put it where the verb normally goes; a two-character verb repeats as a whole word.

tips.title: Verb + 一 + Verb
tips.meaning: Put 一 between two of the same verb to mean do it a little or briefly.
tips.placement: Put it where the verb normally goes, with the object after it.

tips.title: Verb + 了 + Verb
tips.meaning: Put 了 between two of the same verb to say you did something briefly.
tips.placement: Put it where the verb normally goes, with the object after it.

tips.title: Verb + Verb
tips.meaning: Two verbs in a row show two actions happening one after the other, in the order you say them.
tips.placement: Put the first action first, then the second action, right after the subject.
tips.english_note: English adds "and" or "to"; Chinese just puts the two verbs side by side.
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Noun + 去 + Place

tips.title: 我 / 我们
tips.meaning: 我 means I or me; 我们 means we or us.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to say 'my' or 'our'.

tips.title: 你 / 你们
tips.meaning: 你 means you for one person; 你们 means you for two or more people.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to say 'your'.
tips.english_note: English uses 'you' for both; Chinese has two words.

tips.title: 您
tips.meaning: 您 means you, said politely to a teacher or an older person.
tips.placement: Use it where you would use 你.
tips.english_note: English has no polite 'you'.

tips.title: 他 / 她
tips.meaning: 他 means he or him; 她 means she or her.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a family word to say 'his' or 'her'.

tips.title: 他们 / 她们
tips.meaning: 他们 means they or them; 她们 means they or them for a group of women.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the verb, or before a noun to say 'their'.
tips.english_note: English 'they' is one word; Chinese shows who is in the group.

tips.title: Noun as the main statement
tips.meaning: A noun can say what the subject is, with no 是 needed. It often gives time, nationality, or age.
tips.english_note: English needs "is" here, but Chinese can leave it out.

tips.title: 是……的
tips.meaning: It stresses a detail of something that already happened, like when, where, or how.
tips.placement: Put 是 before the detail and 的 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English stresses the detail with voice or "it was...that", but Chinese wraps it in 是 and 的.
structure: Subj. + 是 + Time/Place/Way + Verb + 的
Subj. + 是 + 在 + Place + Verb + 的

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, or a.m.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.
tips.english_note: Chinese says it before the hour, where English puts a.m. after it.

tips.title: 下午
tips.meaning: 下午 means afternoon, or p.m.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.
tips.english_note: Chinese says it before the hour, where English puts p.m. after it.

tips.title: 晚上
tips.meaning: 晚上 means evening or night.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.
tips.english_note: Chinese says it before the hour, where English puts p.m. after it.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and 几点 asks what time it is.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number of the hour.
tips.english_note: English says o'clock after the number too, but Chinese always needs 点.

tips.title: 分
tips.meaning: 分 means minutes.
tips.placement: Put it after the number of minutes, after 点.
tips.english_note: Chinese says the hour first, then the minutes.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 is used to name the days of the week.
tips.placement: Put a number or 几 after it; 星期几 asks which day it is.
structure: 今天 + 是 + 星期 + 几?

tips.title: 年
tips.meaning: 年 means year.
tips.placement: Put the number before it, and put the year first when you say a date.
tips.english_note: Chinese dates go from big to small: year, month, day.
structure: Number + 年 + Number + 月 + Number + 号

tips.title: 月
tips.meaning: 月 means month.
tips.placement: Put the number before it, and the day after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses a number plus 月, not a name like March.

tips.title: 号
tips.meaning: 号 means the day of the month when speaking.
tips.placement: Put it after the number of the day, at the end of the date.
tips.english_note: Chinese says the month first, then the day.

tips.title: 第
tips.meaning: Put 第 before a number to say first, second, third and so on.
tips.placement: It goes right before the number, and a measure word or noun can follow.
tips.english_note: One word 第 works for every number, so there is no -st, -nd, -rd or -th.

tips.title: Verb + person + thing
tips.meaning: Some verbs, like 给, 教 and 告诉, can take two objects: first the person, then the thing.
tips.english_note: English can say 'to' (give a book to her), but Chinese puts the person right after the verb.

tips.title: 次
tips.meaning: 次 counts how many times something happens.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb and the number.

tips.title: 遍
tips.meaning: 遍 counts how many times you do something all the way through, like saying or reading it again.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb and the number.

tips.title: 回
tips.meaning: 回 also means "times" and is a spoken way to count how often something happens.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb and the number.

tips.title: (一)下
tips.meaning: 一下 means doing something briefly or "a little", and it can make a request softer.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.

tips.title: 场
tips.meaning: 场 counts events that happen, like a game, a movie or rain.
tips.placement: Put it after the number, before the event noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses this measure word where English just says "a" or "one".

tips.title: A 比 B + Adj.
tips.meaning: 比 means "than" and compares two things: the first one has more of the quality.
tips.placement: Put 比 between the two things, and the adjective goes last.
tips.english_note: Don't put 很 before the adjective.

tips.title: Verb + 着
tips.meaning: 着 shows an action or state that keeps going, so something stays that way.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English often uses -ing for this, like "smiling" or "standing".

tips.title: Verb + 来/去
tips.meaning: 来 after a verb shows the action moves toward you. 去 shows it moves away from you.
tips.placement: Put 来 or 去 right after the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去
