tips.meaning: Words like 下 and 进 show the direction of the action. Then 来 or 去 shows if it is toward you or away from you.
tips.placement: Put the pair right after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 上/下/进/出/回/过 + 来/去

tips.title: 是不是
tips.meaning: 是不是 asks "is it so, or not?" when you want to check if something is true.
tips.placement: Put it before the main part of a sentence, or add it at the end after a comma.

tips.title: Noun + 呢？
tips.meaning: Add 呢 after a person or thing to ask "what about...?" or "where is...?"
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the short question.
tips.english_note: English says "what about" first, but Chinese just puts 呢 after the word.

tips.title: 快要……了
tips.meaning: Means something is about to happen very soon.
tips.placement: Put 快要 before the verb and 了 at the end.
tips.english_note: English says "about to"; Chinese also needs 了 at the end.

tips.title: 就要……了
tips.meaning: Means something is about to happen very soon.
tips.placement: Put 就要 before the verb and 了 at the end. A time word can go before it.
structure: Time + Subj. + 就要 + Verb + 了

tips.title: 要……了
tips.meaning: Means something is about to happen.
tips.placement: Put 要 before the verb and 了 at the end.
tips.english_note: English says "about to"; Chinese also needs 了 at the end.

tips.title: ……，好吗？
tips.meaning: Added after a suggestion to ask if the other person agrees, like "OK?"
tips.placement: Put it at the very end, after a short pause.

tips.title: ……，可以吗？/ 行吗？
tips.meaning: Added after a request to ask if something is OK or allowed.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end, after a short pause.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: English puts "how" first, but 怎么样 comes at the end.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样？

tips.title: 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪儿 means "where" and is used to ask about a place.
tips.placement: Put it where the place would be in the answer.
tips.english_note: It stays in the same spot as the answer and does not move to the front.

tips.title: 玩儿
tips.meaning: 玩儿 means to play or to have fun.
tips.placement: Use it like a verb such as 去 or 吃.

tips.title: 一会儿
tips.meaning: 一会儿 means a short time, a little while.
tips.placement: Put it after a verb to say the action lasts a short time.

tips.title: 什么时候
tips.meaning: Asks "when" something happens.
tips.placement: Put it where the time word would go, usually before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "when" first, but Chinese keeps it after the subject.
structure: Subj. + 什么时候 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 什么样(的)
tips.meaning: Asks what kind of something, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun it asks about.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么样的 + Noun

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: Asks "why".
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "why" first, but Chinese usually puts it after the subject.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.english_note: You do not need a word for "is" before it.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样?

tips.title: 怎样
tips.meaning: Asks how something is, or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the question, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: You do not need a word for "is" before it.

tips.title: 会
tips.meaning: 会 means can, or knowing how to do something you learned.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
structure: Subj. + 会 + Verb + Obj. + 吗?

tips.title: 能
tips.meaning: 能 means can, when something is possible or allowed.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 上
tips.meaning: 上 means on or on top of something.
tips.placement: Put it right after the thing or place, usually after 在.
tips.english_note: English puts "on" before the noun, but 上 comes after it.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 在 + Noun + 上

tips.title: 里
tips.meaning: 里 means in or inside a place or thing.
tips.placement: Put it right after the place or thing, usually after 在.
tips.english_note: English puts "in" before the noun, but 里 comes after it.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 在 + Place + 里

tips.title: 想
tips.meaning: 想 means "want to" or "would like to" and sounds polite and soft.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb for the thing you want to do.

tips.title: 要
tips.meaning: 要 means "want" or "want to", and it can also mean "going to" or "need to".
tips.placement: Put it before a noun or a verb, and use the situation to pick the meaning.
tips.english_note: English uses different words for these meanings, but Chinese uses just 要.

tips.title: 个
tips.meaning: 个 is the most common measure word, used for people and many everyday things.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and a noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word after a number, even when English doesn't.

tips.title: 块
tips.meaning: 块 means yuan, the basic unit of money in China.
tips.placement: Put it right after a number; 钱 can come after it.

tips.title: 本
tips.meaning: 本 is the measure word for books.
tips.placement: Put it between a number (or 这) and 书.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word between the number and 书, even when English doesn't.

tips.title: 杯
tips.meaning: 杯 is the measure word for a cup or glass of a drink.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the drink.
tips.english_note: It works like "a cup of" in English, but there is no word for "of".

tips.title: 都
tips.meaning: 都 means all or both: everyone or everything in the group does it or is like that.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English puts "all" near the start, but 都 never goes at the start of the sentence.

tips.title: 非常
tips.meaning: 非常 means "very" or "extremely".
tips.placement: Put it right before an adjective.

tips.title: 很
tips.meaning: 很 means "very", but often it just links the subject to an adjective.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.
tips.english_note: English says "is" here, but Chinese uses 很, not 是, before an adjective.

tips.title: 太
tips.meaning: 太 means "too" or "so", for something that is a lot.
tips.placement: Put it before the adjective, and 了 usually comes after the adjective.

tips.title: Number + Measure word + Noun
tips.meaning: Number + Measure word + Noun tells how many things or people there are.
tips.placement: Put the number right before the measure word, and the noun after it.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 两
tips.meaning: 两 means two when you count things.
tips.placement: It goes before a measure word, where 二 is not used.

tips.title: 我
tips.meaning: 我 means I or me.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, or before a family word to mean "my".
tips.english_note: With family words, Chinese just says 我 + the family word, with no 的.

tips.title: 你
tips.meaning: 你 means you.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb as the subject, or after a verb as the object.
tips.english_note: The word stays the same as subject or object.

tips.title: 您
tips.meaning: 您 means you, said politely to teachers or older people.
tips.placement: It goes in the same place as 你.

tips.title: 他
tips.meaning: 他 means he or him.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb as the subject.

tips.title: 她
tips.meaning: 她 means she or her.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb as the subject.

tips.title: 我们
tips.meaning: 我们 means we or us.
tips.placement: It goes in the same place as 我.

tips.title: 正在 / 正
tips.meaning: 正在 means someone is in the middle of doing something at that moment.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: It can mean "is doing" or "was doing", and the verb stays the same.

tips.title: 从
tips.meaning: 从 means "from" and shows where something starts.
tips.placement: Put 从 and the place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says the verb first ("go from here"), but Chinese puts "from + place" before the verb.

tips.title: 这 / 那
tips.meaning: 这 means "this" and 那 means "that".
tips.placement: Put it at the start to point at something, either before 是 or before a measure word and noun.
tips.english_note: Before a noun, Chinese adds a measure word, like 个 or 件.
structure: 这 / 那 + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 这个 / 那个
tips.meaning: 这个 means "this one" and 那个 means "that one".
tips.placement: Use it as the subject at the start of a sentence, or put it before a noun.

tips.title: 这里 / 那里
tips.meaning: 这里 means "here" and 那里 means "there".
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence to say the place.
structure: 这里 / 那里 + 有 / 没有 + Noun

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use 和 only between nouns, not to join two actions.

tips.title: 比
tips.meaning: 比 means "than" and is used to say one thing is more (tall, cheap, big...) than another.
tips.placement: Put 比 between the two things you compare, with the adjective at the end.
tips.english_note: English puts "than" after the adjective, but Chinese puts 比 before it.

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use 和 only to join nouns, not actions.

tips.title: 也
tips.meaning: 也 means "also" or "too".
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English can say "too" at the end, but Chinese never puts 也 at the end.

tips.title: 还
tips.meaning: 还 means "more" or "in addition", adding something to what is already there.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
structure: 还 + 有 + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 的
tips.meaning: 的 links a owner to a thing, like 's in English: 我的 means 'my' and 谁的 means 'whose'.
tips.placement: Put it between the owner and the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 的 where English uses 's or words like my and your.

tips.title: 常常 / 常
tips.meaning: 常常 means "often", and 常 means the same thing.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: Don't put it at the start of the sentence.
structure: Subj. + 常常 / 常 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 再
tips.meaning: 再 means doing something again, or doing some more.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
tips.english_note: Use it for things that have not happened yet.
structure: 再 + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who", and 谁的 means "whose".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The question word stays in the same place as the answer, not at the front.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and is used for small numbers like the time, the date and age.
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go, before a word like 点, 月, 日 or 岁.
tips.english_note: Where English says "what time" or "how old", Chinese just uses 几.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The question word stays in the same place as the answer, not at the front.

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which".
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, such as 个.

tips.title: 哪些
tips.meaning: 哪些 means "which ones" and asks about more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go, often before the verb.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks in what way something is done.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English starts with "how", but Chinese puts 怎么 just before the verb.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much" and asks about an amount.
tips.placement: Put it where the amount would go, such as before 钱.
tips.english_note: To ask a price, Chinese puts 多少 before 钱 and has no word for "is".

tips.title: 哪里 / 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪里 means "where".
tips.placement: Put it where the place would go, for example after 在.
tips.english_note: English puts "where" first, but Chinese puts 哪里 at the end.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. means someone does something, with the verb as the main word of the sentence.
tips.placement: Put the verb right after the subject, and the object after the verb.
tips.english_note: Time words like 明天 or 几点 go before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 了
tips.meaning: 了 means an action is done or has happened.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb when the object has a number or amount, or at the end of a short sentence.
tips.english_note: Chinese verbs never change form, so 了 is what shows the action is finished.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Obj.
Subj. + Verb + Obj. + 了 (+ 吗)?

tips.title: 不
tips.meaning: 不 means "not" or "no" and makes a verb or adjective negative.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: With adjectives, Chinese needs no "is" or "am" before 不.

tips.title: 没(有)
tips.meaning: 没(有) means "did not do" something, or "do not have" or "there is no" something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or noun.

tips.title: Number + Measure word
tips.meaning: Number + Measure word tells how many of something there are, and 几 can replace the number to ask "how many?" or "what time?"
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun, usually after a verb like 有, 要 or 买.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Obj.

tips.title: 在
tips.meaning: 在 means at, in or on a place.
tips.placement: Put 在 + place before the verb, use it alone for where something is, or put it after 住 or 坐.
tips.english_note: English says the place after the verb, but Chinese usually says it before.

tips.title: One-word sentence
tips.meaning: A one-word sentence like 喂 means a whole message all by itself, with no subject or verb.
tips.placement: Say it alone, for example to greet someone or get their attention.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 means the sentence is a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of a normal sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in the statement.
structure: Subj. + 会/想/要 + Verb + Obj. + 吗?

tips.title: 了
tips.meaning: 了 means something has happened or has changed.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence, or right after the object.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a sentence sound like a friendly suggestion.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subject + Verb + Object tells a fact or says what someone does, is or has.
tips.english_note: The verb never changes its form, whoever does it.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Adj. tells what someone or something is like.
tips.placement: Put a word like 很 or 非常 between the subject and the adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese does not use 是 before the adjective.

tips.title: A 比 B + Adj.
tips.meaning: A 比 B + Adj. means A is more (adjective) than B.
tips.placement: Put 比 and the thing you compare with right after the first thing, then the adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese doesn't change the adjective (no -er or "more"); 比 does the comparing.

tips.title: 是
tips.meaning: 是 means 'am', 'is' or 'are' and joins two nouns, like 'he is a teacher'.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns, and add 不 before it to say 'is not'.
tips.english_note: It is used to join nouns, not to describe someone with an adjective.

tips.title: Sentence 1, Sentence 2
tips.meaning: Sentence 1, Sentence 2 means putting two short sentences side by side to give two facts, often a pair that match or contrast.
tips.placement: Put the two sentences next to each other with a comma between them, no joining word needed.
tips.english_note: English often adds 'and' or 'but'; Chinese just places the two sentences together.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., Subj. + Verb + Obj.
Subj. + 是/在 + Noun/Place, Subj. + 是/不在 + Noun/Place

tips.title: 请 + Verb
tips.meaning: 请 means "please" and politely asks someone to do something.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence, right before the verb.
tips.english_note: You don't need to say "you"; just start with 请.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a request or piece of advice sound soft and friendly.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.

tips.title: …了
tips.meaning: 了 at the end of a sentence means something has changed and is now different.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English says "now" or "has become", but Chinese just adds 了.

tips.title: Exclamation sentence (!)
tips.meaning: An exclamation sentence shows strong feeling, such as praise, a greeting, or a goodbye.
tips.placement: Say a short phrase with strong feeling and end it with !

tips.title: 在 + Verb
tips.meaning: 在 means someone is in the middle of doing something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: The verb itself doesn't change; 在 does the job of English "is ...ing".

tips.title: 正在 + Verb
tips.meaning: 正在 means something is happening right now, a little stronger than 在.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: The verb itself doesn't change; 正在 does the job of English "is ...ing".

tips.title: 还是
tips.meaning: 还是 means "or" and lets you ask someone to choose between two options.
tips.placement: Put it between the two options in a question.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 还是 for "or" in questions only.
structure: Option A + 还是 + Option B?
Subj. + Verb + Option A + 还是 + Option B?

tips.title: 有
tips.meaning: 有 means to have, or that there is or there are something somewhere.
tips.placement: Put it before the thing you have, or after the place or time where something is.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 有 for both "have" and "there is/there are".

tips.title: 没有
tips.meaning: 没有 means do not have, or there is not any.
tips.placement: Put it right before the thing that is missing.
tips.english_note: Use 没, not 不, to say no to 有.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement, so nothing moves around like in English.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes-or-no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who", and 谁的 means "whose".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like "who" does.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like "what" does.

tips.title: 几点
tips.meaning: 几点 asks "what time".
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: Time words go before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 哪 + Measure word
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which".
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, in the place of the answer.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 哪 + Measure word (+ Noun)?

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks about a way of doing something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: It goes before the verb, not at the front of the question.

tips.title: 怎么了
tips.meaning: 怎么了 means "What's wrong?".
tips.placement: Put it after the person you are asking about.

tips.title: Number + 块(钱)
tips.meaning: 块 means yuan, the basic unit of Chinese money.
tips.placement: Put a number before it to give a price, and 钱 can follow it.
tips.english_note: The number comes before 块, and no word for "is" is needed.

tips.title: 多少钱
tips.meaning: 多少钱 means "how much money" and is used to ask a price.
tips.placement: Put it after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: The question word stays at the end of the sentence, and no word for "is" is needed.

tips.title: 可能
tips.meaning: 可能 means something may happen or may be true, but you are not sure.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 了
tips.meaning: Verb + 了 means the action was done.
tips.placement: Put 了 right after the verb, before the number and noun.
tips.english_note: English changes the verb to past tense; Chinese keeps the verb and adds 了.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Obj.

tips.title: Sentence + 了
tips.meaning: 了 at the end of a sentence means something has happened or changed.
tips.placement: Put 了 at the end of the sentence, before 吗 in a question.

tips.title: 那么
tips.meaning: 那么 means "so" or "that much", and shows a high degree.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective or verb it describes.

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 means "why" and asks for a reason.
tips.placement: It usually goes after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "why" at the start, but 为什么 comes after the subject.
structure: Subj. + 为什么 + 不 + Verb?

tips.title: Verb + 不/没 + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + 不/没 + Verb, like 有没有, asks a yes-or-no question.
tips.placement: Put it where the verb normally goes, then add the object.
tips.english_note: English adds "do" or "does"; Chinese says the verb twice, with 没 or 不 in between.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and 几点 asks what time it is.
tips.placement: Put a number before 点, and put the time before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word for "at" before the time.

tips.title: 上午 / 下午 / 晚上 / 早上
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, 下午 means afternoon, 晚上 means evening, and 早上 means early morning.
tips.placement: Put them before the hour.
tips.english_note: They come before the clock time, not after it like "a.m." or "p.m."
structure: Subj. + 上午 / 下午 / 晚上 + Number + 点 + Verb

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 means week, and 星期 + a number, 天 or 日 names a day of the week.
tips.placement: Put 几 after 星期 to ask which day it is.
structure: Time + 是 + 星期 + Number / 天 / 日

tips.title: 条
tips.meaning: 条 is a measure word for long, thin things, like pants, roads, and fish.
tips.placement: Put it between the number and the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a pair of pants" or just "two fish", but Chinese needs a measure word between a number and a noun.

tips.title: 千
tips.meaning: 千 means thousand.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, and a measure word or noun usually comes after.

tips.title: 万
tips.meaning: 万 means ten thousand.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, and a measure word or noun usually comes after.
tips.english_note: English has no single word for ten thousand, so think of 万 as its own unit.

tips.title: 只
tips.meaning: 只 means "only" or "just" and shows there is a small amount or no more than that.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who"; 谁的 means "whose".
tips.placement: Put 谁 in the spot where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front like "who" in English.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what"; 什么时候 means "when".
tips.placement: Put 什么 in the spot where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how"; 怎么了 asks "what's wrong?".
tips.placement: Put 怎么 right before the verb.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "what number" and is used for time, dates and days.
tips.placement: Put 几 where the number would go.
tips.english_note: English says "what time" or "what day"; Chinese just uses 几 with the measure word.

tips.title: 哪(个)
tips.meaning: 哪个 means "which one".
tips.placement: Put 哪个 where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front.

tips.title: 哪里 / 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪里 means "where".
tips.placement: Put 哪里 where the place would go.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much".
tips.placement: Put 多少 right before the thing you ask about, such as 钱.

tips.title: 经常
tips.meaning: 经常 means something happens often.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 已经
tips.meaning: 已经 means something has already happened or is already true.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, and put 了 at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: 自己
tips.meaning: 自己 means 'myself', 'himself', 'herself' or 'themselves', the same person as the subject.
tips.placement: It can go right after a person word, or after a verb as the object.
tips.english_note: One word 自己 works for myself, yourself, himself and so on.

tips.title: 大家
tips.meaning: 大家 means everyone in the group.
tips.placement: It goes where a subject goes, at the start of the sentence.

tips.title: 它
tips.meaning: 它 means 'it', for one animal or thing.
tips.placement: It goes where a subject or an object goes.
tips.english_note: 它 is only for animals and things, not for people.

tips.title: 它们
tips.meaning: 它们 means 'they', for more than one animal or thing.
tips.placement: It goes where a subject or an object goes.
tips.english_note: 它们 is only for animals and things, not for people.

tips.title: 往
tips.meaning: 往 means "towards" and shows which direction you do something in.
tips.placement: Put 往 and the direction word before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the direction after the verb ("look up"), but Chinese puts it before.

tips.title: 就
tips.meaning: 就 means "then": the first part gives a situation, and the second part says what happens or what to do next.
tips.placement: Put 就 right before the verb in the second part.
tips.english_note: English often says "then" at the start, but 就 goes before the verb.
structure: 如果 + Situation, Subj. + 就 + Verb

tips.title: Verb + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + Verb means doing something a little, or for a short time, in a casual way.
tips.placement: It goes where the single verb would go; for a two-character verb, repeat the whole word.
tips.english_note: Where English says "a little" or "a bit", Chinese just repeats the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 一 + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + 一 + Verb means doing something a little or briefly, and it sounds light and relaxed.
tips.placement: Put 一 between the two copies of a one-character verb.

tips.title: Verb + 了 + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + 了 + Verb means someone did something a little or briefly, and it is already done.
tips.placement: Put 了 between the two copies of a one-character verb.

tips.title: 从
tips.meaning: 从 means "from" and shows where something starts.
tips.placement: Put 从 + place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "from" after the verb, but Chinese puts 从 and the place before the verb.

tips.title: 给
tips.meaning: 给 means 'to' or 'for' and shows who an action is aimed at.
tips.placement: Put 给 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the person after the verb ('call you'), but Chinese puts 给 + person before it.

tips.title: 离
tips.meaning: 离 means 'from' when you say how far or close one place is to another.
tips.placement: Put it between the two places, before 近 or 远.
tips.english_note: English puts 'from' after 'far'; Chinese puts 离 before the adjective.
structure: Place 1 + 离 + Place 2 + 很 + 近/远

tips.title: Verb + 得 + Adj.
tips.meaning: 得 links an action to a description of how well or how it is done.
tips.placement: Put 得 right after the verb, then add the description.
tips.english_note: English says "slept well" with no extra word; Chinese puts 得 between the verb and the description.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 得 + 很 + Adj.

tips.title: 对
tips.meaning: 对 means "to" or "toward" someone or something, showing who an action or feeling is aimed at.
tips.placement: Put 对 and the person before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English says "talk to him", but Chinese puts 对 + person before the verb.

tips.title: 分钟
tips.meaning: 分钟 means minutes, and it tells how long something lasts.
tips.placement: Put it after a number, right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for"; the time length just comes after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 分钟 + Obj.

tips.title: 年
tips.meaning: 年 means years, and it tells how long something lasts.
tips.placement: Put it after a number, right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for"; it needs no extra measure word after the number.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 年 + Obj.

tips.title: 天
tips.meaning: 天 means days, and it tells how long something lasts.
tips.placement: Put it after a number, right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for"; the time length just comes after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 天 + Obj.

tips.title: 周
tips.meaning: 周 means weeks, and it tells how long something lasts.
tips.placement: Put it after a number, right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word for "for"; the time length just comes after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + 周 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 着 + Verb
tips.meaning: 着 after a verb shows how someone does a second action, like smiling while looking.
tips.placement: Put 着 right after the first verb, then add the main action verb.
tips.english_note: English often uses "-ing" or "while" for the first verb.

tips.title: Verb + 过
tips.meaning: 过 means you have done something at least once before, or have had that experience.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no extra word like "ever" or "before"; 过 does that job.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 at the end of a sentence turns it into a friendly suggestion, like "let's" or "how about".
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English says "let's" at the start; Chinese just adds 吧 at the end, often with 我们.

tips.title: 喂
tips.meaning: 喂 means "hello" and is used to start or answer a phone call.
tips.placement: Put it at the very start, before what you say next.
tips.english_note: 喂 is mainly for phone calls, not for greeting people face to face.

tips.title: 但 / 但是
tips.meaning: 但 and 但是 mean "but" and show that the second part goes against the first.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the second part, after the first part.

tips.title: 什么的
tips.meaning: 什么的 means "and so on" and ends a list of things, when the listener can guess what else you mean.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the list, after the last item.
tips.english_note: English puts "and so on" after the list too, but Chinese often has no "and" before the last item.
structure: Verb + Obj. 1 + Verb + Obj. 2 + 什么的

tips.title: Verb + 得 + Adj.
tips.meaning: Verb + 得 + Adj. tells how well or in what way someone does an action.
tips.placement: Put 得 right after the verb, then the adjective, usually with 很 before it.
tips.english_note: English puts 'well' or 'fast' after the action as a separate word; Chinese joins it to the verb with 得.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 得 + 很 + Adj.

tips.title: 次
tips.meaning: 次 means "times" and counts how often an action happens.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, with a number before it.

tips.title: 遍
tips.meaning: 遍 counts how many times you do something from start to finish, like saying or reading it through.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, with a number before it.

tips.title: 回
tips.meaning: 回 means "times" and counts how often an action happens, especially in everyday speech.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, with a number before it.

tips.title: 一下
tips.meaning: 一下 means doing an action briefly or "a little", and it can make the sentence sound softer.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.

tips.title: 场
tips.meaning: 场 counts a whole event, such as a movie, a game, or a rainstorm.
tips.placement: Put it after a number and before the noun.

tips.title: 还是……吧
tips.meaning: 还是……吧 means "had better": you compare the choices and suggest the better one.
tips.placement: Put 还是 before the verb and 吧 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 还是 and 吧 together where English says "had better" or "let's".
structure: Subj. + 还是 + Verb + Obj. + 吧

tips.title: Noun or number phrase without 是
tips.meaning: Subj. + Noun means the subject is that thing, with no 是 needed, like a day, the weather or an age.
tips.placement: Put the noun or number phrase right after the subject.
tips.english_note: English needs "is" here, but Chinese just puts the two parts side by side.

tips.title: Noun as the sentence's main statement
tips.meaning: Subj. + Noun means the noun alone says what the subject is, like its time, weather, origin or age.
tips.placement: Put the noun right after the subject, with no 是 needed.
tips.english_note: English needs "is", but Chinese can leave out 是 here.

tips.title: 有(一)点(儿)
tips.meaning: 有点 means "a bit" and is often used for things you don't like.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 挺
tips.meaning: 挺 means "quite" or "pretty", as in "pretty good".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, often with 的 at the end.

tips.title: 更
tips.meaning: 更 means "even more".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 更 before the adjective instead of adding "-er" to it.

tips.title: 特别
tips.meaning: 特别 means "especially" or "very".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 十分
tips.meaning: 十分 means "very" or "extremely".
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.

tips.title: 多么
tips.meaning: 多么 means "how" and shows strong feeling about something.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, often with 啊 at the end.
tips.english_note: English says "How pretty!" and Chinese uses 多么 the same way.

tips.title: 多
tips.meaning: 多 means "how" or "so" when you feel strongly about something.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective, often with 啊 at the end.

tips.title: 好
tips.meaning: 好 means "so" or "very" in everyday speech.
tips.placement: Put it before an adjective.
tips.english_note: Here 好 is not "good"; it makes the adjective stronger.

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: Verb + 一下 means doing the action briefly or a little, which makes it sound light and easy.
tips.placement: Put 一下 right after the verb, before any object.
tips.english_note: English often just uses the plain verb, or adds "a bit" or "a moment".

tips.title: 比
tips.meaning: 比 means "than" and compares two things.
tips.placement: Put it between the two things, with the adjective after the second one.
tips.english_note: English puts "than" after the adjective, but 比 comes before it.

tips.title: Verb + 好
tips.meaning: Verb + 好 means the action is done well or done completely.
tips.placement: Put 好 right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English uses a separate word like "well"; Chinese attaches 好 straight to the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 晚
tips.meaning: Verb + 晚 means the action happened too late.
tips.placement: Put 晚 right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "late" after the verb too, but Chinese joins 晚 directly to the verb.

tips.title: Place + Verb + 着 + Noun
tips.meaning: 着 after a verb like 放, 站 or 坐 says that something or someone is sitting, standing or lying in a place.
tips.placement: Put the place first, then the verb with 着, then the thing or person that is there.
tips.english_note: Chinese starts with the place, and the thing that is there comes last.

tips.title: Verb + direction word (来/去)
tips.meaning: Verb + 来/去 means the action moves toward the speaker (来) or away from the speaker (去).
tips.placement: Put the direction word right after the verb, and 上, 下 or 起 can go before 来 or 去.
tips.english_note: English often says only up or down, but Chinese adds 来 or 去 to show toward or away from you.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 上/下/起 + 来/去

tips.title: Adj. + 一点(儿)
tips.meaning: 一点儿 means a little, and after an adjective it means a little more of that quality.
tips.placement: Put it right after the adjective.
tips.english_note: Where English changes the adjective (quicker, better), Chinese keeps the adjective the same and adds 一点儿.

tips.title: 是……的
tips.meaning: 是……的 points out a detail of something that already happened, like when, where or how.
tips.placement: Put 是 before the detail and 的 at the end, after the verb.
tips.english_note: English stresses the detail with the voice or says "it was ... that"; Chinese uses 是……的.
structure: Subj. + 是 + Time/Place/Way + Verb + 的
Subj. + 是 + 在 + Place + Verb + 的

tips.title: 有 + amount
tips.meaning: 有 means someone or something reaches a certain amount, like a height or an age.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, right before the number.
tips.english_note: Where English says "is" (he is 1.8 meters tall), Chinese uses 有.
structure: Subj. + 有 + Number + Measure word + Adj.
Subj. + 有 + Number + 多 + 岁

tips.title: Verb + person + thing
tips.meaning: Verb + person + thing means one action has two objects: you give, teach, or tell someone something.
tips.placement: Put the person first, then the thing, right after verbs like 给, 教, and 告诉.
tips.english_note: Chinese does not need "to" before the person, like English "give the ticket to me."
structure: 请 + 给 + 我 + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 一……就……
tips.meaning: 一……就…… means that as soon as one thing happens, another thing happens right after, or every time the first happens, the second follows.
tips.placement: Put 一 before the first verb and 就 before the second verb.
tips.english_note: English says "as soon as" or "every time" at the start; Chinese puts 一 and 就 right before the two verbs.
structure: Subj. 1 + 一 + Verb 1，Subj. 2 + 就 + Verb 2

tips.title: Verb + Obj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Verb + Obj. + Verb + Obj. means one person does two actions in a row, such as going by bus, or going somewhere to do something.
tips.placement: Put the actions in the order they happen, with nothing between them.
tips.english_note: English adds "and" or "to" between the actions, but Chinese just puts the verbs side by side.
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Noun + 去 + Place

tips.title: 第 + Number
tips.meaning: 第 turns a number into 'first', 'second', 'third' and so on.
tips.placement: Put 第 right before the number, then add a measure word such as 次.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 第 for every number, with no endings like -st, -nd or -th.
structure: Subj. + 是 + 第 + Number + Measure word

tips.title: Verb + 过
tips.meaning: Verb + 过 means you have done this before, at some time in the past.
tips.placement: Put 过 right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: English says "have done"; Chinese just adds 过 after the verb and the verb does not change.
structure: Subj. + 没(有) + Verb + 过 + Obj.

tips.title: A,还是 B?
tips.meaning: 还是 means "or" when you ask someone to pick one of two choices.
tips.placement: Put it between the two choices, and end the whole sentence as a question.
tips.english_note: The question does not need 吗.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Noun 1 + 还是 + Verb + Noun 2?

tips.title: 但(是)
tips.meaning: 但 and 但是 mean "but" and show that the second part goes against the first part.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the second part, after a comma.

tips.title: 因为……所以……
tips.meaning: 因为……所以…… means "because ... so ..." and links a reason to its result.
tips.placement: Put 因为 before the reason, then 所以 before the result.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses both words in one sentence, but English uses only one of "because" or "so".
structure: 因为 + Reason, 所以 + Result

tips.title: Verb + 着
tips.meaning: Verb + 着 means an action or state is continuing, like "smiling" or "standing".
tips.placement: Put 着 right after the verb, and a second verb can follow to show what else is happening.
tips.english_note: English uses "-ing" or "while"; Chinese just adds 着 after the first verb.

tips.title: 就 / 就是
tips.meaning: 就 means "exactly" or "right", and it stresses that something is just as you say.
tips.placement: Put it right before 是 or 在, after the subject.
tips.english_note: English shows this by stressing a word, like "right here" or "exactly"; Chinese adds 就.

tips.title: Statement + 吧?
tips.meaning: Statement + 吧? means you guess something is true and want the other person to confirm it.
tips.placement: Put 吧 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English uses a tag like "right?" or "isn't it?", but Chinese just adds 吧 at the end.

tips.title: 是不是
tips.meaning: 是不是 turns a sentence into a question that asks "is it so or not?"
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun or phrase you are asking about, in place of 是.
tips.english_note: English uses "Is he...?" or "...or not?", but Chinese puts 是 and 不是 together.

tips.title: 哪儿 / 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪儿 means "where" and is used to ask about a place.
tips.placement: Put it in the spot where the place would go in the answer.
tips.english_note: The word does not move to the front like "where" in English.

tips.title: 快要……了
tips.meaning: 快要 means something is about to happen soon.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb and end the sentence with 了.

tips.title: 就要……了
tips.meaning: 就要 means something is about to happen very soon.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, after the subject or a time word, and end the sentence with 了.
structure: Subj. + Time + 就要 + Verb + 了

tips.title: 好吗
tips.meaning: 好吗 means "OK?" and asks if the other person agrees with your suggestion.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of your sentence, after a comma.

tips.title: 可以吗
tips.meaning: 可以吗 means "Is that OK?" and asks if the other person agrees or allows it.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of your sentence, after a comma.

tips.title: 行吗
tips.meaning: 行吗 means "Will that do?" and asks if the other person is OK with your idea.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of your sentence, after a comma.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 means "how is it?" and asks what something is like or what someone thinks.
tips.placement: Put it after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 怎么样 at the end, where English puts "how" first.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样？

tips.title: Number + 多
tips.meaning: 多 after a number means "more than" that number.
tips.placement: Put it right after a number like 十, 百 or 千, before the measure word.
tips.english_note: English says "more than" before the number, but Chinese puts 多 after it.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "a few" and is not an exact number.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, or after it add 十, 百, 千 or 万 for "a few tens, hundreds…".
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word after 几.
structure: 几 + 十/百/千/万 + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 左右
tips.meaning: 左右 means "about" or "around" the number before it.
tips.placement: Put it after the number and its measure word.
tips.english_note: English says "about" before the number, but Chinese puts 左右 after it.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + 左右 (+ Noun)

tips.title: 什么时候
tips.meaning: 什么时候 means "when" and asks about a time.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, where the time word would go in the answer.
tips.english_note: English puts "when" first, but Chinese keeps it in the middle of the sentence.
structure: Subj. + 什么时候 + Verb (+ Obj.)?

tips.title: 什么样
tips.meaning: 什么样 means "what kind of" and asks what someone or something is like.
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun, with 的 in between.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么样 + 的 + Noun?

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 means "why" and asks for a reason.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb or adjective you are asking about.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 means "how is it?" and asks what something is like or what someone thinks of it.
tips.placement: Put it at the end, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English starts with "how" or "what", but Chinese puts the question word last.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样?

tips.title: 怎样
tips.meaning: 怎样 means "how" and asks how something is or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put it at the end, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English starts with "how", but Chinese puts the question word last.

tips.title: Sentence 1, Sentence 2
tips.meaning: Sentence 1, Sentence 2 means two short sentences side by side, each saying something about a different person or thing.
tips.placement: Put them next to each other with a comma between.
tips.english_note: English often adds 'and' or 'but'; Chinese can just place the two sentences together.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. means someone does something.
tips.placement: Put the verb right after the subject, and the object right after the verb.
tips.english_note: To say no, put 不 or 没 before the verb, and the order stays the same.

tips.title: 什么的
tips.meaning: 什么的 means "and so on" and ends a list of things.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the list, after the last item.
tips.english_note: English says "and so on" after the list too, but 什么的 is more casual.

tips.title: Verb + 得 + Adj.
tips.meaning: Verb + 得 + Adj. tells you how an action goes, for example how well someone sleeps or runs.
tips.placement: Put 得 right after the verb, then add a word like 很 and the adjective.
tips.english_note: English uses an adverb after the verb; Chinese uses 得 plus an adjective.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 得 + 很 + Adj.

tips.title: Noun/number phrase as sentence
tips.meaning: A noun or number phrase can be the main part of a sentence, telling the time, date, weather or amount.
tips.placement: Put it right after the subject, with no 是.
tips.english_note: English needs "is" here, but Chinese often leaves it out.

tips.title: 就
tips.meaning: 就 means "then": the first part gives a situation, and the second part says what happens or what to do next.
tips.placement: Put 就 right before the verb in the second part.
tips.english_note: English often leaves out "then", but Chinese likes to keep 就.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + 很 + Adj. says what someone or something is like.
tips.placement: Put the adjective right after the subject, often with 很 or 非常 before it.
tips.english_note: Chinese does not use 是 ("is") before the adjective.

tips.title: Noun as the statement
tips.meaning: Noun + Noun means the second noun tells what the subject is, with no 是 needed.
tips.english_note: English needs "is", but here the noun can follow the subject directly.

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: 一下 means do something a little or for a short moment, and it makes the sentence sound softer.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English uses words like "a bit" or "a moment", but Chinese just adds 一下 after the verb.

tips.title: 是……的
tips.meaning: 是……的 points out a detail of something that already happened, like when, where or how.
tips.placement: Put the detail right after 是, and put 的 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English stresses the detail with its voice, but Chinese puts it between 是 and 的.
structure: Subj. + 是 + Time/Place/Way + Verb + 的
Subj. + 是 + 在 + Place + Verb + 的

tips.title: Verb + person + thing
tips.meaning: Verb + person + thing means someone gives, tells or teaches a person something, using verbs like 给, 教 and 告诉.
tips.placement: Put the person right after the verb, then the thing.
tips.english_note: No word like "to" goes between them.

tips.title: Number + Measure word
tips.meaning: Number + Measure word tells how many of something there are.
tips.placement: Put it right before the noun, often after verbs like 有, 要 and 买.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word like 个 between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 几 + Measure word
tips.meaning: 几 means 'how many' or 'what number' and asks about a small number, like in 几点 and 几岁.
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go in the answer.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 几 + Measure word + Noun?

tips.title: Verb + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + Verb means doing something a little or briefly, in a casual way.
tips.placement: Repeat the whole verb, whether it has one or two characters, where the verb normally goes.
tips.english_note: English says "a little" or "a bit"; Chinese just repeats the verb.

tips.title: Verb + 一 + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + 一 + Verb means doing something a little or briefly, and sounds light and friendly.
tips.placement: Put 一 between the two same verbs.

tips.title: Place + Verb + 着 + Noun
tips.meaning: 着 after a verb means someone or something is there in that state, like sitting or standing.
tips.placement: Put the place first, then the verb with 着, then who or what is there.
tips.english_note: English says "There is...", but Chinese just starts with the place.

tips.title: Verb + 来/去
tips.meaning: Verb + 来/去 shows which way an action goes: 来 is toward the speaker, 去 is away from the speaker.
tips.placement: Add 上 or 下 before 来/去 to also say up or down.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 上/下 + 来/去

tips.title: 一……就……
tips.meaning: 一……就…… means as soon as one thing happens, the next thing happens right after.
tips.placement: Put 一 before the first verb and 就 before the second verb.
tips.english_note: English says "as soon as" once, but Chinese uses both 一 and 就.
structure: Subj. + 一 + Verb, + 就 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + Obj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Verb + Obj. + Verb + Obj. means two actions happen one after the other.
tips.placement: Say the first action first, then the second, both after the subject.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no "and" or "to" between the two actions.
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Noun + 去 + Place

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who", and 谁的 means "whose".
tips.placement: Put 谁 where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English puts "who" first, but 谁 stays in the usual spot.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what", and 什么时候 means "when".
tips.placement: Put 什么 where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English puts "what" first, but 什么 stays in the usual spot.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how", and 怎么了 asks what is wrong.
tips.placement: Put 怎么 before the verb.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks about a small number, like the time or the date.
tips.placement: Put 几 where the number would go.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 几 for time and date, where English says "what".

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which".
tips.placement: Put 哪 before a measure word, where the answer would go.

tips.title: 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪里 means "where".
tips.placement: Put 哪里 where the place would go.
tips.english_note: English puts "where" first, but 哪里 stays in the usual spot.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much", and it can ask about any size of number.
tips.placement: Put 多少 where the number would go.

tips.title: 快要……了
tips.meaning: 快要 means something is about to happen soon, and 了 at the end shows the change is coming.
tips.placement: Put 快要 before the verb and 了 at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English says "about to" before the verb, but Chinese also needs 了 at the end.

tips.title: 就要……了
tips.meaning: 就要 means something is about to happen very soon, and 了 at the end shows the change is coming.
tips.placement: Put 就要 before the verb, after the subject or the time, with 了 at the end.
structure: Subj. + Time + 就要 + Verb + 了

tips.title: 好吗
tips.meaning: 好吗 asks if the other person agrees with your idea or request.
tips.placement: Say your idea first, then put 好吗 at the very end.
tips.english_note: It works like "OK?" added to the end of an English sentence.

tips.title: 可以吗
tips.meaning: 可以吗 asks if something is allowed or fine with the other person.
tips.placement: Say what you want to do first, then put 可以吗 at the very end.
tips.english_note: It works like "Is that OK?" or "May I?" added to the end.

tips.title: 行吗
tips.meaning: 行吗 asks if something is OK with the other person.
tips.placement: Say your idea first, then put 行吗 at the very end.
tips.english_note: It works like "OK?" added to the end of an English sentence.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 asks how something is or what it is like.
tips.placement: Put the thing you ask about first, then 怎么样 at the end.
tips.english_note: English starts with "how", but 怎么样 comes last, and it needs no 吗.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样？

tips.title: 什么时候
tips.meaning: 什么时候 means "when" and asks about time.
tips.placement: It goes where the time word would go, usually after the subject.
tips.english_note: English puts "when" first, but Chinese keeps it in the normal time spot.
structure: Subj. + 什么时候 + Verb + Obj. ?

tips.title: 什么样
tips.meaning: 什么样 means "what kind of" and asks about the type or look of something.
tips.placement: Put it before 的 and a noun, in the spot where the noun would be.
tips.english_note: English moves "what kind of" to the front, but Chinese keeps it in the object's spot.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 什么样 + 的 + Noun ?

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 means "why" and asks for a reason.
tips.placement: It usually goes at the start or right before the verb.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 means "how is it?" and is a question about what something is like.
tips.placement: It goes at the end, right after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word for "is" here; just put 怎么样 after the topic.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样 ?

tips.title: 怎样
tips.meaning: 怎样 means "how" and asks what something is like.
tips.placement: It usually goes after the thing you are asking about.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word for "is" here; just put 怎样 after the topic.

tips.title: 都
tips.meaning: 都 means "all" or "both" and covers everyone or everything you are talking about.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English puts "all" first, but 都 never starts the sentence.

tips.title: 很
tips.meaning: 很 means very, but it often just links a subject to an adjective.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese does not use 是 before an adjective; 很 takes that place.

tips.title: 非常
tips.meaning: 非常 means very, very much, and makes an adjective stronger.
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.

tips.title: 太
tips.meaning: 太 means too, as in too much.
tips.placement: Put it before the adjective, and 了 at the end.
tips.english_note: English has no word like this 了 at the end.

tips.title: 个
tips.meaning: 个 is the most common measure word, used for people and many everyday things.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word after a number, where English just says "three children".

tips.title: 本
tips.meaning: 本 is the measure word for books.
tips.placement: Put it between a number (or 这) and 书.

tips.title: 杯
tips.meaning: 杯 is the measure word for a cup or glass of a drink.
tips.placement: Put it between a number and the drink.
tips.english_note: It works like "a cup of" or "a glass of" in English.

tips.title: 块
tips.meaning: 块 is the everyday word for yuan, the Chinese money unit.
tips.placement: Put it after the number of yuan.

tips.title: Number + Measure word + Noun
tips.meaning: Number + Measure word + Noun tells how many of something there are, using numbers like 一, 二, 五, 十.
tips.placement: Put the number right before the measure word, and put the whole group where you would put the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese usually puts a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use 和 only for nouns, not for joining two actions or whole sentences.

tips.title: 想
tips.meaning: 想 means want to or would like to do something.
tips.english_note: The verb comes right after 想, with no word for "to".

tips.title: 要
tips.meaning: 要 means want something or want to do something, and it can also mean will or need to.
tips.placement: Put 要 after the subject, before the noun or verb.
tips.english_note: The verb comes right after 要, with no word for "to".

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.
tips.english_note: Use 和 only for nouns, not to join two actions.

tips.title: 我
tips.meaning: 我 means I, me, or my.
tips.placement: Put it before a verb to say what you do, or before a family word to say 'my'.
tips.english_note: No 的 is needed between 我 and a family word.

tips.title: 你
tips.meaning: 你 means you, for one person.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb as the subject, or after a verb as the object.
tips.english_note: 你 stays the same as subject or object.

tips.title: 您
tips.meaning: 您 means you, said politely to one person.
tips.placement: Use it for someone you respect, such as a teacher.

tips.title: 他
tips.meaning: 他 means he or him.
tips.placement: It goes where the subject goes, before the verb.

tips.title: 她
tips.meaning: 她 means she or her.
tips.placement: It goes where the subject goes, before the verb.

tips.title: 我们
tips.meaning: 我们 means we or us.
tips.placement: It goes where the subject goes, before the verb.

tips.title: 不
tips.meaning: 不 means "not" and says that something is not true or is not done.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or adjective.

tips.title: 没(有)
tips.meaning: 没(有) means "didn't do" something, or "don't have" or "there is no" something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses the same word for "didn't" and for "no" or "don't have".

tips.title: 在
tips.meaning: 在 means to be at a place, or to do something at a place.
tips.placement: To say where you do something, put 在 and the place before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts the place after the verb, but Chinese puts it before.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. is the basic Chinese sentence: someone does something, or something happens.
tips.placement: Put the verb right after the subject, and the object right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Time words like 明天 and 几点 go before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who", and 谁的 means "whose".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a normal sentence, so 谁 does not move to the front.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and is used to ask about small numbers, like the time, the date or age.
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go.
tips.english_note: Chinese asks "how many o'clock" where English asks "what time".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 几 + Measure word + Noun?

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what".
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English moves "what" to the front, but 什么 stays in place.

tips.title: 哪(个)
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which".
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, such as 个.

tips.title: 哪些
tips.meaning: 哪些 means "which ones" and asks about more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.

tips.title: 哪里 / 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪里 means "where".
tips.placement: Put it where the place would go.
tips.english_note: English moves "where" to the front, but 哪里 stays in place.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks the way to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "how" at the start, but 怎么 goes before the verb.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much".
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go.

tips.title: 了
tips.meaning: 了 means an action is finished or done.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb when the object has a number, or at the end of a short sentence or question.
tips.english_note: The verb itself never changes; 了 shows the action is done.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Obj.

tips.title: 这 / 那
tips.meaning: 这 means this, and 那 means that.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence, before 是.

tips.title: 这个 / 那个
tips.meaning: 这个 means this one, and 那个 means that one.
tips.placement: It can stand alone as the subject, or go right before a noun.

tips.title: 这 / 那 + Measure word + Noun
tips.meaning: 这 / 那 + Measure word + Noun means "this ..." or "that ..." for a specific thing.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts a measure word between 这 / 那 and the noun.
structure: 这 / 那 + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 这里 / 那里
tips.meaning: 这里 means here, and 那里 means there.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence to say where something is.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement; you just add 吗.

tips.title: 了 (end of sentence)
tips.meaning: 了 means something has happened or has changed.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The verb does not change; 了 shows the new situation or finished action.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a sentence sound like a gentle suggestion.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Adj. says what someone or something is like.
tips.placement: The adjective goes right after the subject, and words like 很, 非常 or 太 usually go before it.
tips.english_note: Chinese doesn't need 是 (is/am/are) before the adjective.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. means a plain statement that tells a fact.
tips.placement: Put the subject first, then the verb, then the object.
tips.english_note: To describe something, you can put an adjective right after the subject, with no 是.

tips.title: 是
tips.meaning: 是 means "am / is / are" and joins two nouns, like 'A is B'.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns, with 也 or 都 just before it.
tips.english_note: Chinese 是 links nouns, so don't use it before an adjective.

tips.title: Two short sentences side by side
tips.meaning: Two short sentences side by side means you say two related things together, often to compare or contrast them.
tips.placement: Put the two sentences next to each other with a comma between them.
tips.english_note: English often adds 'and' or 'but' between them, but Chinese doesn't need a word.
structure: Subj. + 是 + Noun, Subj. + 是 + Noun.

tips.title: 请 + Verb
tips.meaning: 请 means "please" and politely asks someone to do something.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the sentence, right before the verb.
tips.english_note: You don't need to say "you" before the verb.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a command sound soft and friendly, like a suggestion.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.

tips.title: Sentence + ！
tips.meaning: Sentence + ！ means you say something with strong feeling, like a greeting, a goodbye, or being pleased.
tips.placement: Put ！ at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: Number + Measure word
tips.meaning: Number + Measure word says how many of something there are.
tips.placement: Put it before the noun, and use 几 in the number's place to ask a question, such as 几点 for the time.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 有
tips.meaning: 有 means to have, or that something is there.
tips.placement: Put it before the thing you have or the thing that is there.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 有 for both "have" and "there is/there are".

tips.title: 没有
tips.meaning: 没有 means do not have, or there is none.
tips.placement: Put it before the thing that is missing.
tips.english_note: Use 没 with 有, not 不.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes/no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as the statement; you just add 吗.

tips.title: Verb + 了
tips.meaning: 了 means an action has happened or is done.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, or at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The verb itself does not change; 了 is added instead of a past form like "drank".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 了 + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: Noun/Pronoun + 呢？
tips.meaning: 呢 after a noun or pronoun makes a short question that means "what about...?" or "how about...?".
tips.placement: Put it at the end, after the person or thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English says "what about you?", but Chinese needs only the word and 呢.

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: Verb + 一下 means doing something briefly, just a little, or for a moment.
tips.placement: Put 一下 right after the verb, before any object.
tips.english_note: English often just uses the plain verb, or adds "a bit" or "for a moment".

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a statement into a yes-or-no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The rest of the sentence keeps its normal word order.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means who, and 谁的 means whose.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go; 谁的 goes before the noun.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means what.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like English "what".

tips.title: 几 (几点)
tips.meaning: 几点 asks what time it is, or what time something happens.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, before the verb.

tips.title: 怎么了
tips.meaning: 怎么了 asks what is wrong or what happened.
tips.placement: Put it after the person you ask about.

tips.title: 哪个
tips.meaning: 哪个 means which one.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like English "which".

tips.title: 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪里 means where.
tips.placement: Put it after 在, where the place would go.
tips.english_note: It stays at the end instead of moving to the front.

tips.title: Verb + Obj. + Verb
tips.meaning: Verb + Obj. + Verb means one person does two actions, one after the other, in the order you say them.
tips.placement: Put the verbs in the order they happen, with the same subject before both.
tips.english_note: English adds 'to', 'by' or 'and' between the actions, but Chinese just puts them side by side.
structure: Subj. + 坐 + Noun + 去 + Place

tips.title: Verb + person + thing
tips.meaning: Verb + person + thing means giving, teaching or telling someone something, with verbs like 给, 教 and 告诉.
tips.placement: Put the person right after the verb, then the thing.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word like "to" before the person.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and 几点 asks what time it is.
tips.placement: Put a number before 点 to say the hour, and put the time before the verb.
tips.english_note: The time usually comes before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 半
tips.meaning: 半 means half, so 点 + 半 means half past the hour.
tips.placement: Put 半 right after 点.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 means week, and 星期 with a number or 天 names a day of the week.
tips.placement: Put 星期 before the number, and use 星期几 to ask which day.
tips.english_note: Sunday is 星期天 or 星期日, not a number.

tips.title: 上午 / 早上
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, and 早上 means early morning.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: The time of day comes before the hour, with no "a.m." after it.
structure: Subj. + 上午/早上 + Number + 点 + Verb

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means who, and 谁的 means whose.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It stays in the same place as the answer, not at the start like English "who".

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means what.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like English "what". 什么时候 means when.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means how many or which number, and is used for time, dates and days.
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go.
structure: 今天 + 几 + 月 + 几 + 号？

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means how, and 你怎么了 asks what is wrong.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 哪 + Measure word
tips.meaning: 哪 means which.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, then the noun if needed.
tips.english_note: You need a measure word after 哪, like 哪个.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 哪 + Measure word (+ Noun)？

tips.title: 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪里 means where.
tips.placement: Put it where the place would go.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front like English "where".

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means how many or how much.
tips.placement: Put it before the noun it asks about.

tips.title: Two short sentences in a row
tips.meaning: Two short sentences side by side means you compare or contrast two things, like two people or two places.
tips.placement: Put the two parts next to each other, with a comma between them.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no word like "and" or "but" between the two parts.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj., Subj. + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + (很) + Adj. tells you what the subject is like.
tips.placement: Put the adjective right after the subject, often with 很, 非常 or 太 in front of it.
tips.english_note: Chinese does not use 是 (is) before the adjective.

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: 一下(儿) means doing an action briefly or just a little, and it makes the request or suggestion softer.
tips.placement: Put it right after the verb, before the object.

tips.title: Noun + 呢？
tips.meaning: 呢 means "what about...?" and asks a question about the person or thing right before it.
tips.placement: Say the person or thing first, then put 呢 at the end.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs no words for "what about"; 呢 does that job.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. tells what someone does.
tips.placement: Put 不 or 没 before the verb to say no.
tips.english_note: The verb stays the same, whoever does it and whenever.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. makes a simple statement about who does or is something.
tips.english_note: Word order is much like English, and the verb never changes.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who" and asks about a person.
tips.placement: Put 谁 where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English moves "who" to the front, but 谁 stays in the answer's spot.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what" and asks about a thing; 什么时候 asks "when".
tips.placement: Put 什么 where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English puts "what" first, but 什么 stays in the answer's spot.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks about a small number, such as the time, day, or date.
tips.placement: Put 几 where the number would go, like before 点, 月, or 号.
tips.english_note: English says "what time", but Chinese asks "how many o'clock" with 几点.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks how something is done; 怎么了 asks what is wrong.
tips.placement: Put 怎么 before the verb.

tips.title: 哪 + Measure word
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which" and asks you to pick one from several.
tips.placement: Put 哪 before a measure word, where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: English says "which" before a noun, but Chinese puts a measure word after 哪.

tips.title: 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪里 means "where" and asks about a place.
tips.placement: Put 哪里 where the answer place would go.
tips.english_note: English puts "where" first, but 哪里 stays in the answer's spot.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much" and asks about an amount.
tips.placement: Put 多少 before the noun; 多少钱 asks the price.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. is a plain sentence that tells a fact or says what someone does.
tips.placement: Start with who or what, then the verb, then the object.

tips.title: Subj. + (很) + Adj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + (很) + Adj. tells what someone or something is like.
tips.placement: Put a word like 很 or 非常 before the adjective.
tips.english_note: Mandarin does not put 是 ("is") before the adjective.

tips.title: Subj. + Verb + Obj.
tips.meaning: Subj. + Verb + Obj. tells what someone does.
tips.placement: Words like 能, 会, 想, 要, 没 go right before the verb.
tips.english_note: The verb never changes, whoever does it and whenever it happens.
structure: Subj. + 想/会/要/没 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 一起
tips.meaning: 一起 means doing something together with other people.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "together" after the verb, but Chinese puts 一起 before it.

tips.title: 都
tips.meaning: 都 means all or both, for more than one person or thing.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject and before the verb or adjective.
tips.english_note: English "all" can come first, but 都 never starts the sentence.

tips.title: Number + 块
tips.meaning: 块 means the basic unit of money, like a yuan or a dollar.
tips.placement: Put it right after the number.
tips.english_note: The word for the money comes after the number, and 钱 can follow it.

tips.title: 钱 / 多少钱
tips.meaning: 钱 means money, and 多少钱 asks how much something costs.
tips.placement: Put 多少钱 after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no word like "is" here: the thing comes first, then 多少钱.

tips.title: 个
tips.meaning: 个 means one item or person; it is the most common measure word and goes with many nouns.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这 and before the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun, but English doesn't.

tips.title: 块
tips.meaning: 块 means yuan, the basic unit of Chinese money.
tips.placement: Put it after the number; 钱 can follow it.

tips.title: 家
tips.meaning: 家 is the measure word for shops, restaurants and other businesses.
tips.placement: Put it after a number and before the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a shop"; Chinese puts 家 between the number and the noun.

tips.title: 本
tips.meaning: 本 is the measure word for books and notebooks.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这 and before the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs 本 between the number and the book; English doesn't.

tips.title: 杯
tips.meaning: 杯 means cup or glass and counts drinks.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这 and before the drink.
tips.english_note: It is like "a cup of" in English, but Chinese doesn't need a word for "of".

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two things.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "with" and shows who you do something with.
tips.placement: Put 跟 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "with" after the verb, but Chinese puts 跟 before it.

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "with" and tells who you do something with.
tips.placement: Put 跟 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English puts "with" after the verb, but Chinese puts it before.
structure: Subj. + 跟 + Noun + 一起 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 上 / 上边
tips.meaning: 上 means on or on top of something.
tips.placement: Put it after the noun for the thing, usually after 在.
tips.english_note: English says "on" before the noun, but Chinese puts 上 after it.

tips.title: 下 / 下边
tips.meaning: 下 means under or below something.
tips.placement: Put it after the noun for the thing, usually after 在.
tips.english_note: English says "under" before the noun, but Chinese puts 下 after it.
structure: Noun + 在 + Noun + 下 / 下边

tips.title: 里 / 里边
tips.meaning: 里 means in or inside something.
tips.placement: Put it after the noun for the place or container, usually after 在.
tips.english_note: English says "in" before the noun, but Chinese puts 里 after it.

tips.title: 不
tips.meaning: 不 means "not" and makes a verb or an adjective negative.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or adjective.

tips.title: 别
tips.meaning: 别 means "don't" and tells someone not to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 没(有)
tips.meaning: 没(有) means something did not happen, or you do not have something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb or the noun.

tips.title: 太
tips.meaning: 太 means too, or very much.
tips.placement: Put 太 before an adjective, and 了 usually comes at the end.

tips.title: 很
tips.meaning: 很 means very, but it often just links the subject to an adjective.
tips.placement: Put 很 right before the adjective.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 很 where English just says "is", so no 是 is needed.

tips.title: 最
tips.meaning: 最 means the most.
tips.placement: Put 最 before an adjective or before a verb like 喜欢.

tips.title: 真
tips.meaning: 真 means really.
tips.placement: Put 真 right before the adjective.

tips.title: 非常
tips.meaning: 非常 means very.
tips.placement: Put 非常 right before the adjective.

tips.title: 快要……了
tips.meaning: 快要 means something is about to happen very soon.
tips.placement: Put 快要 before the verb and 了 at the end.
tips.english_note: English has no word like 了 to close the sentence, but Chinese uses it here.

tips.title: 就要……了
tips.meaning: 就要 means something is about to happen soon, and it can go with a time like next month.
tips.placement: Put the time first, then 就要 before the verb, and 了 at the end.
structure: Subj. + Time + 就要 + Verb + 了

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, the time from sunrise until noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: It comes before the hour, where English puts "a.m." after it.

tips.title: 星期 / 星期天 / 星期日
tips.meaning: 星期 means week, and 星期天 and 星期日 both mean Sunday.
tips.placement: Put 几 after 星期 to ask which day of the week it is.
structure: Time + 是 + 星期天/星期日。

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and it comes after the number of the hour.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, or use 几点 to ask the time.
tips.english_note: A time like 七点 goes before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪儿 means "where" and asks about a place.
tips.placement: Put it in the spot where the place would be in the answer.
tips.english_note: It does not move to the front of the sentence like "where" does.

tips.title: 玩儿
tips.meaning: 玩儿 means to play or to have fun.
tips.placement: It goes after the subject, and a place like 在门口 comes before it.

tips.title: 哪儿
tips.meaning: 哪儿 means "where" and is used to ask about a place.
tips.placement: Put it where the place would go in the answer.
tips.english_note: It stays in the same spot as the answer, not at the start of the sentence.

tips.title: 玩儿
tips.meaning: 玩儿 means "to play" or "to have fun".
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, with a place before it if you need one.

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "with" a person.
tips.placement: Put 跟 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says "with" after the verb, but Chinese puts it before the verb.

tips.title: 了
tips.meaning: 了 means something has happened or changed, like it is done or it is now different.
tips.placement: Put it after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: English shows this with past tense or words like 'now' and 'already'; Chinese just adds 了.

tips.title: 吗
tips.meaning: 吗 turns a sentence into a yes-or-no question.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as a normal sentence.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a friendly suggestion, like 'let's' or 'why not'.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.
