tips.title: 呢
tips.meaning: 呢 means 'and what about...?' when you ask back about someone or something.
tips.placement: Put it after the noun or the word for the person.

tips.title: Verb + 一下(儿)
tips.meaning: Verb + 一下 means doing something briefly or just a little, which makes the sentence sound light and casual.
tips.placement: Put 一下 right after the verb, before the object if there is one.

tips.title: Commands and requests
tips.meaning: Commands and requests tell or ask someone to do something, or not to do it.
tips.placement: Put 请 (please) or 别 (don't) before the verb, and 吧 at the end to suggest doing something together.
tips.english_note: You usually leave out the subject 你, as in English.

tips.title: Verb + 好
tips.meaning: Verb + 好 means you do the action well or finish it properly.
tips.placement: Put 好 right after the verb.

tips.title: Verb + result word
tips.meaning: Verb + result word tells how an action turned out, such as late, wrong or clean.
tips.placement: Put the result word right after the verb, and 了 often comes after it.
tips.english_note: English says the result as a separate word, but Chinese puts it right after the verb.

tips.title: Questions with 吗 and question words
tips.meaning: Adding 吗 to a sentence, or using a question word like 谁 or 什么, makes it a question.
tips.placement: 吗 goes at the end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: A question word stays where the answer would be, not at the front.

tips.title: 再
tips.meaning: 再 means doing something again or more, after now; 不再 means no longer.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 经常 / 常常 / 常
tips.meaning: 经常, 常常 and 常 all mean you do something often.
tips.placement: Put them before the verb, after the subject.
structure: Subj. + 经常/常常 + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: A,还是 B?
tips.meaning: A,还是 B? means "A or B?" and asks the other person to choose between two options.
tips.placement: Put 还是 between the two choices.
structure: Verb + Obj. 1 + 还是 + Verb + Obj. 2?
Subj. + Verb + Noun 1 + 还是 + Noun 2?

tips.title: ..., 但(是) ...
tips.meaning: A sentence with 但 or 但是 means "but": the second part goes against what the first part says.
tips.placement: Put 但 or 但是 at the start of the second part, usually after a comma.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Obj.，但是 + Subj. + Verb + Obj.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what" and asks about things.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go, either alone or before a noun.
tips.english_note: The question word stays in place and does not move to the front.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks for a small number, like a time, date or age.
tips.placement: Put it where the number would go, before the measure word or time word.
tips.english_note: Where English says "what time" or "what day", Chinese uses 几.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 几 + Measure word + Noun?
几 + 月 / 号 / 点 / 岁

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which" and asks you to choose one.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, like 哪个, or before 位 for a person.

tips.title: 哪些
tips.meaning: 哪些 means "which ones" and asks about more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the things would be, as the subject or before a noun.

tips.title: 哪儿 / 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪儿 and 哪里 mean "where" and ask about a place.
tips.placement: Put it where the place would go, often after 在.
tips.english_note: The question word stays at the end, not at the front like in English.
structure: Noun + 在 + 哪儿 / 哪里?

tips.title: 多 + Adj.
tips.meaning: 多 before an adjective like 长 or 大 asks "how long" or "how big".
tips.placement: Put it right before the adjective.
tips.english_note: English uses "how" plus an adjective; Chinese uses 多 plus the adjective.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much" and asks about any amount.
tips.placement: Put it before the noun, or after the thing in 多少钱.
tips.english_note: For price, Chinese says the thing first, then 多少钱.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks the way to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: 你怎么了 is a set question meaning "What's wrong?"

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who" and asks about a person.
tips.placement: Put it where the person would go; add 的 to ask "whose".
tips.english_note: The question word stays in place and does not move to the front.

tips.title: 一 二 三 四 五 六 七 八 九
tips.meaning: 一, 二, 三, 四, 五, 六, 七, 八 and 九 mean one to nine.
tips.placement: Put the number before a measure word, then the noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun.
structure: Subj. + Verb + Number + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 两
tips.meaning: 两 means two when you count things.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word.
structure: Subj. + 有 + 两 + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: 十
tips.meaning: 十 means ten, and it helps build bigger numbers.
tips.placement: Put a number after 十 to add, or before 十 to multiply.
tips.english_note: Twelve is ten-two, and twenty is two-ten.

tips.title: 百
tips.meaning: 百 means hundred.
tips.placement: Put a number before it, and a measure word after it.

tips.title: 零
tips.meaning: 零 means zero.
tips.placement: With 点, 零点 means midnight.

tips.title: 半
tips.meaning: 半 means half.
tips.placement: Put it after 点 for half past the hour, or before a measure word like 年.
tips.english_note: For half past nine, Chinese puts 半 after the hour.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 半 + 年 + Obj.

tips.title: 几 / 多少 questions
tips.meaning: 几 and 多少 ask 'how many' or 'what number' in place of a number.
tips.placement: Put the question word exactly where the answer number would go.
tips.english_note: The question word does not move to the front.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 几 + Measure word + Noun

tips.title: Commands and requests
tips.meaning: Commands and requests tell someone to do something, and 请 makes them polite.
tips.placement: Start with the verb, or put 请 first, and leave out the subject.

tips.title: 吗 and question words
tips.meaning: 吗 at the end of a sentence makes it a yes/no question, and question words like 什么, 谁, 几 and 哪儿 ask for missing information.
tips.placement: A question word goes in the spot where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement, so the question word does not move to the front.

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what" and asks about things.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The word does not move to the front like "what" does in English.

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks about small numbers, like time, dates and age.
tips.placement: Put it before words like 点, 月, 号 and 岁.
tips.english_note: Chinese asks "how many o'clock" instead of "what time".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 几 + 点/月/号/岁?

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which" and asks you to choose one.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word.

tips.title: 哪些
tips.meaning: 哪些 means "which ones" and asks about more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go, before a noun or alone.

tips.title: 哪儿 / 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪儿 and 哪里 mean "where".
tips.placement: Put them at the end, after 在 or a verb.
tips.english_note: The word stays at the end, not at the front like "where".

tips.title: 多 + Adj.
tips.meaning: 多 + Adj. means "how (big, old...)" and asks about degree.
tips.placement: Put 多 right before the adjective.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much" and asks about amounts.
tips.placement: Put it before a noun, or after the noun when asking a price with 钱.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks the way to do something; 怎么了 asks "what's wrong?"
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who" and asks about a person.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The word does not move to the front like "who" does in English.

tips.title: Questions with 吗 / question words
tips.meaning: Questions use 吗 or a question word like 什么 or 谁 to ask yes/no or for information.
tips.placement: Put 吗 at the end, or put the question word where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: The word order stays the same as in a statement.

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 means "why" and asks for a reason.
tips.placement: It usually goes after the subject and before the verb, or at the start of the question.
tips.english_note: English puts "why" first, but in Chinese it usually comes after the subject.

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 means "how is it?" and asks what something is like or what someone thinks of it.
tips.placement: It goes at the end of the question, after the thing you ask about.
tips.english_note: English puts "how" first, but Chinese puts 怎么样 last.
structure: 你觉得 + Noun + 怎么样?

tips.title: 件
tips.meaning: 件 is the measure word for clothes like shirts and coats, and also for things like matters.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这/那/哪 and before the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "one shirt", but Chinese needs a measure word between the number and the noun.

tips.title: 位
tips.meaning: 位 is a polite measure word for people.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这/那/哪 and before the noun, or use it alone when asking who someone is.
tips.english_note: English has no polite word like this to count people.

tips.title: 条
tips.meaning: 条 is the measure word for long, thin things like pants, skirts, and roads.
tips.placement: Put it after a number or 这/那/哪 and before the noun.
tips.english_note: English says "a pair of pants", but Chinese uses 条 for the one long item.

tips.title: 有时
tips.meaning: 有时 means sometimes.
tips.placement: Put it after the subject, before the verb.

tips.title: 正在
tips.meaning: 正在 means someone is doing something right now.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no -ing ending, so 正在 before the verb does that job.

tips.title: 正
tips.meaning: 正 means something is happening right now.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb; 着 and 呢 often come along with it.
tips.english_note: Chinese has no -ing ending, so 正 before the verb does that job.
structure: Subj. + 正 + Verb + 着 + Obj. + 呢

tips.title: 在
tips.meaning: 在 means someone is doing something right now.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: English changes the verb to "-ing"; Chinese keeps the verb the same and adds 在 before it.

tips.title: 正在
tips.meaning: 正在 means someone is doing something right at this moment.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.

tips.title: 正
tips.meaning: 正 is a short way to say 正在, meaning something is happening right now.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb; 呢 at the end of the sentence often goes with it.
structure: Subj. + 正 + Verb + 着 + Obj. + 呢

tips.title: 和
tips.meaning: 和 means "and" and joins two nouns.
tips.placement: Put it between the two nouns.

tips.title: 跟
tips.meaning: 跟 means "with" and goes before the person you do something with.
tips.placement: Put 跟 and the person before the verb.
tips.english_note: The "with" part comes before the verb, not after it.

tips.title: 还是
tips.meaning: 还是 means "or" and asks someone to choose between two options.
tips.placement: Put it between the two options.
structure: Option A + 还是 + Option B ?
Subj. + Verb + Option A + 还是 + Option B ?

tips.title: 这么 / 那么
tips.meaning: 这么 and 那么 mean "so" or "this/that much"; 这么 feels close, 那么 feels farther away.
tips.placement: Put it right before an adjective.
structure: Subj. + 这么 / 那么 + Adj.
Subj. + 有 + Noun + 这么 / 那么 + Adj. + 吗?

tips.title: 这样 / 那样
tips.meaning: 这样 means "this way" and 那样 means "that way".
tips.placement: Put it before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts "this way" before the verb, while English often puts it after.
structure: Subj. + 这样 / 那样 + Verb (+ Obj.)

tips.title: 我
tips.meaning: 我 means I, me or my.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun to show it is yours.
tips.english_note: One word does the work of I, me and my.

tips.title: 你
tips.meaning: 你 means you or your, for one person.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun to show it belongs to the person you are talking to.
tips.english_note: One word does the work of you and your.

tips.title: 您
tips.meaning: 您 means you, said politely to a teacher or an older person.
tips.placement: It goes where 你 goes, often right after a title.
tips.english_note: English has no polite form of you.

tips.title: 他
tips.meaning: 他 means he, him or his, for a man or boy.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun to show it is his.
tips.english_note: One word does the work of he, him and his.

tips.title: 她
tips.meaning: 她 means she, her or hers, for a woman or girl.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun to show it is hers.
tips.english_note: One word does the work of she and her.

tips.title: 我们
tips.meaning: 我们 means we, us or our.
tips.placement: It goes before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun to show it is ours.
tips.english_note: One word does the work of we, us and our.

tips.title: 你们
tips.meaning: 你们 means you or your, for two or more people.
tips.placement: It goes where 你 goes: before a verb, after a verb, or before a noun.
tips.english_note: English uses the same word for one person or many; Chinese has 你们 for many.

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, the time before noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: English says a.m. after the time, but Chinese says 上午 first.

tips.title: 下午
tips.meaning: 下午 means afternoon, the time after noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: English says p.m. after the time, but Chinese says 下午 first.

tips.title: 晚上
tips.meaning: 晚上 means evening or night.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour, after a day word like 明天.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and 几点 asks what time it is.
tips.placement: Put the number before 点, and put the whole time before the verb.
tips.english_note: The time usually goes before the verb, not at the end.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 means week, and 星期 + a number names a day of the week.
tips.placement: Use 星期 + 一 to 六 for Monday to Saturday, and 星期几 to ask which day.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses numbers for the days, not separate names.

tips.title: 星期天 / 星期日
tips.meaning: 星期天 and 星期日 both mean Sunday.
tips.placement: Put it near the start, before the verb.
tips.english_note: English says on Sunday, but Chinese needs no word for on.

tips.title: 第 + Number
tips.meaning: 第 means 'number...' or 'the ...th'. It turns a number into an order, like first, second, third.
tips.placement: Put it right before the number, then add a measure word and a noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 第 for every number, so there is no -st, -nd, -th ending.
structure: Subj. + 是 + 第 + Number + Measure word

tips.title: 吧 (asking to check)
tips.meaning: 吧 turns a statement into a question when you guess something is true and want the listener to agree.
tips.placement: Put 吧 at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: One 吧 does the job of English endings like "don't you?" or "isn't it?".

tips.title: 但 / 但是
tips.meaning: 但 and 但是 mean "but" and introduce something that goes against what you just said.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the second part, after a comma.

tips.title: 虽然
tips.meaning: 虽然 means "although" and gives the first fact, which the second part then goes against.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the first part, and start the second part with 但.
tips.english_note: English uses either "although" or "but", but Chinese often uses both 虽然 and 但.

tips.title: 吧
tips.meaning: 吧 makes a sentence softer: it turns an order into a suggestion, or a question into a guess you want to check.
tips.placement: Put it at the very end of the sentence.
tips.english_note: In a question it works like English "right?" or "isn't it?"

tips.title: 啊
tips.meaning: 啊 makes a sentence sound friendly, casual or full of feeling.
tips.placement: Put it at the end of the sentence.

tips.title: 已经
tips.meaning: 已经 means "already": something has happened or is true earlier than you might expect.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, adjective or time, and end the sentence with 了.
tips.english_note: With 不, it means "not any more".

tips.title: 还
tips.meaning: 还 means "still": something keeps going on and has not stopped.
tips.placement: Put it before the verb, often with 在.

tips.title: Verb + 好
tips.meaning: Verb + 好 means an action is finished and done well, so things are ready.
tips.placement: Put 好 right after the verb; 没 goes before the verb to say it is not ready yet.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 好 (+ Obj.) + 了

tips.title: Verb + 完
tips.meaning: Verb + 完 means you finish doing the action.
tips.placement: Put 完 right after the verb, before the object.
tips.english_note: English says "finish" alone, but Chinese puts 完 after the real verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 完 (+ Obj.) + 了
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 完 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 懂
tips.meaning: Verb + 懂 means you do the action and understand it.
tips.placement: Put 懂 right after the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese often says "hear-understand" where English says just "understand".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 懂 + Obj. + 了
Subj. + 没 + Verb + 懂 + Obj.

tips.title: Verb + 错
tips.meaning: Verb + 错 means you did the action wrongly, by mistake.
tips.placement: Put 错 right after the verb.
tips.english_note: English uses words like "wrongly" or "mis-"; Chinese puts 错 after the verb.
structure: Subj. + Verb + 错 + 了 (+ Obj.)

tips.title: 什么
tips.meaning: 什么 means "what" and asks about a thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It stays in the sentence and does not move to the front like "what".

tips.title: 谁
tips.meaning: 谁 means "who" and asks about a person.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.
tips.english_note: It stays in the sentence and does not move to the front like "who".

tips.title: 哪
tips.meaning: 哪 means "which" and asks you to choose one.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word, then the noun.

tips.title: 哪些
tips.meaning: 哪些 means "which ones" and asks about more than one thing.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer would go.

tips.title: 哪儿 / 哪里
tips.meaning: 哪儿 and 哪里 mean "where" and ask about a place.
tips.placement: Put it where the answer place would go, often after 在.
tips.english_note: It stays in the sentence and does not move to the front like "where".
structure: Subj. + Verb + 在 + 哪儿/哪里?

tips.title: 几
tips.meaning: 几 means "how many" and asks about a small number, like time or date.
tips.placement: Put it before a measure word.

tips.title: 多少
tips.meaning: 多少 means "how many" or "how much" and asks about any amount.
tips.placement: Put it before a noun, or after a noun to ask the price.

tips.title: 怎么
tips.meaning: 怎么 means "how" and asks the way to do something.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: It can also show surprise, like "how come".

tips.title: 怎么样
tips.meaning: 怎么样 means "how is it" and asks what something is like.
tips.placement: Put it at the end, after the thing you ask about.

tips.title: 为什么
tips.meaning: 为什么 means "why" and asks for a reason.
tips.placement: Put it at the start of the question, or use it alone.

tips.title: Adj. + 一点(儿)
tips.meaning: 一点儿 means a little or a bit more.
tips.placement: Put it right after the adjective to make a small difference or a polite request.

tips.title: Adj. + 多了
tips.meaning: 多了 means much more.
tips.placement: Put it after the adjective, with or without 比.
tips.english_note: English puts "much" before the adjective, but Chinese puts 多了 after it.
structure: A + 比 + B + Adj. + 多了

tips.title: Adj. + 得多
tips.meaning: 得多 means much more.
tips.placement: Put it right after the adjective in a 比 sentence.
tips.english_note: English puts "much" before the adjective, but Chinese puts 得多 after it.
structure: A + 比 + B + Adj. + 得多

tips.title: 大/小 + Number + 岁
tips.meaning: 岁 means years old, and after 大 or 小 it says how many years older or younger.
tips.placement: Put the number and 岁 right after 大 or 小.
tips.english_note: English says "older" at the end, but Chinese puts the number of years after 大 or 小.
structure: A + 比 + B + 大/小 + Number + 岁

tips.title: 在
tips.meaning: 在 means someone is doing something right now.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb.
tips.english_note: The verb does not change, so there is no -ing ending.

tips.title: 正在
tips.meaning: 正在 means an action is happening at this very moment.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb, just like 在.
tips.english_note: It can also describe a moment in the past, like "was doing" in English.

tips.title: 正
tips.meaning: 正 is a short form of 正在 and means the action is happening right now.
tips.placement: Put it right before the verb, and 呢 often comes at the end.
structure: Subj. + 正 + Verb + Obj. + 呢

tips.title: 第
tips.meaning: 第 turns a number into an order word, like first, second or third.
tips.placement: Put it right before the number, then add a measure word and a noun.
tips.english_note: Chinese uses 第 for every order word, with no endings like -st or -nd.
structure: Subj. + 是 + 第 + Number + Measure word

tips.title: 第 + Number
tips.meaning: 第 + Number means the first, second or third one in order.
tips.placement: Use it alone to give a rank, or add a measure word like 个, 次 or 天 after it.
structure: 第 + Number + 次 / 天 / 名

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, the hours before noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 上午 before the hour, where English puts a.m. after it.

tips.title: 下午
tips.meaning: 下午 means afternoon, the hours after noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 下午 before the hour, where English puts p.m. after it.

tips.title: 晚上
tips.meaning: 晚上 means evening or night.
tips.placement: Put it before the hour, after a day word like 明天.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts 晚上 before the hour, where English puts it after.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 means week, and 星期 + a number names a day, like 星期一 for Monday. 星期天 and 星期日 both mean Sunday.
tips.placement: Put the day near the start of the sentence, before the time.
tips.english_note: To ask the day, say 星期几, which is like "week which".

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and a number goes before it.
tips.placement: Put the time before the verb.
tips.english_note: Chinese puts the time before the verb, where English often puts it at the end.

tips.title: 上午
tips.meaning: 上午 means morning, the hours before noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.
tips.english_note: Chinese says 上午 before the hour where English says "a.m." after it.

tips.title: 下午
tips.meaning: 下午 means afternoon, the hours after noon.
tips.placement: Put it before the clock time.
tips.english_note: Chinese says 下午 before the hour where English says "p.m." after it.

tips.title: 晚上
tips.meaning: 晚上 means evening or night.
tips.placement: Put it after a day word like 明天 and before the clock time.
tips.english_note: It comes before the hour, not after it.

tips.title: 星期
tips.meaning: 星期 plus a number names a day of the week, and 星期天 or 星期日 means Sunday.
tips.placement: Put the day at the start of the sentence or after the subject.
tips.english_note: You don't need a word for "on" before the day.

tips.title: 点
tips.meaning: 点 means o'clock, and 几点 asks what time it is.
tips.placement: Put the number before 点, and put the time before the verb.
tips.english_note: The time usually comes before the verb, not at the end of the sentence.
